prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that periodically reads moisture levels from a DFRobot Soil Moisture Sensor v2.0, an analog resistive sensor, via an MCP3008 analog-to-digital converter connected over the SPI bus. Wire the MCP3008 to the Pi's hardware SPI0 bus: chip enable CE0 on GPIO8, MOSI on GPIO10, MISO on GPIO9, and SCLK on GPIO11, with the sensor's analog output wired to MCP3008 channel 0 (CH0). Use the pigpio library for all SPI communication with the ADC. Sample the raw 10-bit ADC value, in the range 0-1023, once per second, and log each reading to the console together with a timestamp so the moisture trend can be reviewed later. Implement robust error handling around SPI initialization and every SPI transfer, reporting any failure rather than silently continuing. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for a graceful shutdown, making sure the SPI handle is closed and pigpio is terminated cleanly on every exit path, including early failures.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads current from an MLX91219 Hall-effect current sensor, which has an analog output, via an ADS1115 analog-to-digital converter over I2C, using the pigpio library for all I2C communication. Wire the ADS1115's ADDR pin to GND, giving it I2C address 0x48 on bus 1; wire the MLX91219's analog output to the ADS1115's AIN0 input; and wire the ADS1115's SDA and SCL lines to the Pi's GPIO2 and GPIO3. Configure the ADS1115 for single-shot mode, AIN0 single-ended (MUX=100), a programmable gain amplifier setting of PGA ±4.096V, and a data rate of 128 samples per second. Every 500ms, log the computed current in amperes to the console, deriving it from the MLX91219's sensitivity of 40mV/A with its zero-current offset centered at mid-supply. Access the ADS1115's 16-bit registers with i2cWriteI2CBlockData and i2cReadI2CBlockData, respecting the correct byte order, and handle I2C write and read errors as well as sensor-absent paths gracefully rather than crashing. On SIGINT, close the I2C handle and call gpioTerminate() before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ to interface with an AZDelivery KY-026 Flame Sensor Module and an MCP3008 ADC via SPI, using the pigpio library only (do not use wiringPi). Read the KY-026 digital output (D0) on GPIO4 (BCM numbering) and sample its analog output (A0) on MCP3008 channel 0 (single-ended); connect the MCP3008 to SPI0 (CE0/GPIO8) at 1 MHz. Approximate ambient temperature from the analog reading using a linear map of the 10-bit ADC value (0-1023) to 10-40°C. Once per second, log timestamped CSV rows (Timestamp,FlameDetected,Temperature) to flame_data.csv. Implement robust error handling: verify pigpio initialization, SPI open/transfer, and file operations; on sensor-absent or SPI-failure paths, skip the log entry and print a diagnostic. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that monitors two sensors and activates a buzzer when both indicate a fire condition simultaneously, using the pigpio library for all GPIO and I2C access. Connect a Keyes KY-026 Flame Sensor's digital output to GPIO4, using the internal pull-up resistor; the sensor outputs LOW when a flame is detected. Connect an LM393-based Heat Sensor's analog output to an ADS1115 ADC on I2C bus 1 at address 0x48, channel AIN0 (single-ended), configured for single-shot mode, gain ±4.096V, 128 SPS (conversion time ~8.5ms); map the ADC voltage range 0V-3.3V linearly to 20°C-80°C and treat above 60°C as a trigger. Connect the buzzer to GPIO27, active HIGH. Poll the flame sensor and read the temperature every 100ms. Implement a 50ms debounce on the flame sensor using a falling-edge ISR callback, registering a flame event only if at least 50ms have elapsed since the last accepted event. If both a debounced flame event and temperature above 60°C occur together, log the event with a timestamp to fire_log.txt and sound the buzzer for 2 seconds. If only flame is detected, log "Flame detected!"; if only the temperature exceeds 60°C, log the temperature reading. If the ADC read fails (I2C error or sensor absent), log an error and continue without crashing. Check the return values of pigpio initialization, I2C open, the ADC configuration write, the ADC read, and log file creation, printing descriptive errors to stderr for each failure path; on any initialization failure, release all resources acquired so far and exit with code 1. Handle SIGINT by setting a running flag to 0 so the main loop exits cleanly, then turn off the buzzer, deregister the ISR, close the I2C handle, close the log file, and call gpioTerminate(). Use only pigpio, never wiringPi or libgpiod; drive the buzzer with a simple digital write rather than PWM; and ensure the code compiles cleanly with gcc -Wall, with no undeclared identifiers or implicit declarations.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W to interface with a Melexis MLX90817 absolute pressure sensor over I2C bus 1 at 7-bit address 0x40, using the pigpio library for I2C. Once per second, read the 16-bit pressure value from register 0x00 and convert it to pressure in kPa using pressure_kPa = (raw_value / 65535.0) * 500.0. Log each reading with an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp to a comma-separated file named pressure_log.csv with columns timestamp,pressure_kPa, opening the file once at startup with a header row rather than on every write, and flushing after each write. Check every pigpio/I2C call and file operation for errors; on an I2C read failure, print an error to stderr with the register and the pigpio error code, and continue the loop without logging. Handle sensor-absent scenarios, including I2C open failure or repeated read failures. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler to cleanly close the I2C handle, flush and close the log file, and call gpioTerminate() before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to interface with a Melexis MLX90834 pressure sensor. The MLX90834 is a SENT-only MEMS pressure sensor with no native I2C interface, so read its analog pressure output via a generic I2C ADC bridge, an ADS1115 at address 0x48, using the pigpio library for both I2C and GPIO. Configure the ADS1115 to read single-ended on AIN0 (pressure signal) and AIN1 (NTC temperature signal) at a gain of 2/3 (FSR ±6.144V), 128 SPS. Convert the ADC voltage to pressure using a linear transfer function (0V = 0 kPa, 5V = 400 kPa) and to temperature using a simplified linear NTC approximation (1V = 0°C, 2V = 100°C). Every 1 second, display the pressure (kPa) and temperature (°C) on the console, and drive a warning LED on GPIO17 (active-high) HIGH when pressure exceeds 105.0 kPa. Implement robust error handling: validate every pigpio call, retry failed I2C reads up to 3 times, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths. Ensure clean resource release on SIGINT.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads motor current using a Melexis MLX91209 Hall-effect current sensor (analog output) via an MCP3008 10-bit SPI ADC, using only the pigpio library (no wiringPi). Connect the MLX91209 analog output to MCP3008 channel 0 (single-ended), with the MCP3008 on SPI0 CE0 (GPIO8 CE, GPIO11 SCLK, GPIO10 MOSI, GPIO9 MISO) at 1 MHz, SPI mode 0. The MCP3008 protocol uses a 3-byte transfer: a start bit (0x01), a single-ended channel configuration byte, and a zero pad byte; extract the 10-bit result from the last two bytes of the response. Convert the 10-bit ADC reading to a voltage (0-3.3V full-scale, 1024 steps), then to current using the sensor's zero-current midpoint at Vcc/2 and a sensitivity of 66 mV/A. Sample every 100ms and log each reading with a timestamp to current_log.txt in append mode, flushing after every write. Implement a safety monitor: if current exceeds 10A, assert GPIO27 HIGH to trigger a motor shutdown, log an OVERCURRENT event, and stop the program. Handle all error paths: pigpio initialization failure, SPI open/transfer errors, invalid ADC values, and file I/O errors. On SIGINT/SIGTERM, cleanly close the SPI handle, close the log file, reset GPIO27 to LOW, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ to interface with a Honeywell MICROceL MCO-S4 CO sensor whose analog voltage output is read via an external MCP3008 ADC connected to the Pi's hardware SPI0 bus (CE0 on BCM GPIO8, SCLK on BCM 11, MOSI on BCM 10, MISO on BCM 9), with the CO sensor's analog output wired to MCP3008 channel 0. Use the pigpio library, not wiringPi, to configure the SPI bus at 1 MHz (SPI mode 0) and to control an alarm on BCM GPIO4. Read the ADC continuously, once per second, convert the 10-bit ADC value to a voltage using a 3.3V reference, and drive the alarm on BCM GPIO4 HIGH if the voltage exceeds 2.5V, or LOW if it is 2.5V or below. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W to monitor a potted plant using a HiLetgo Soil Moisture Sensor (analog resistive sensor) connected to an MCP3008 ADC, reading it via SPI using the pigpio library (never wiringPi). Wire the MCP3008 on SPI CE0 (bus 0, channel 0) at 500 kHz, single-ended mode, reading ADC channel 0, with the HiLetgo sensor's analog output connected to MCP3008 CH0 and its VCC at 3.3V. Calibrate raw ADC value 300 as 0% moisture (dry air) and 700 as 100% moisture (immersed in water), with lower raw values indicating drier soil. Every 60 seconds, log the timestamp and moisture percentage to plant_data.txt in the format YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, <moisture_percent>, appending each entry. If moisture drops below 30%, trigger an email alert via msmtp, piping the email body via popen (not system with shell interpolation), and validate the msmtp exit status. Accept command-line arguments for the SPI channel, ADC channel, minimum/maximum raw calibration values, moisture threshold, logging frequency in seconds, recipient email, and the msmtp config file path. Check every initialization call and SPI transfer for errors, printing diagnostics to stderr; if an ADC read fails, log the error to stderr and retry on the next cycle without crashing. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown: close the SPI connection, terminate pigpio, free all dynamically allocated memory, and exit cleanly on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously monitors soil moisture using a Keyes KY-036 analog sensor, using the pigpio library (not wiringPi). Read the KY-036's analog output (A0) via an MCP3008 10-bit SPI ADC (single-ended mode, channel 0), connected on SPI0 (CE0, GPIO8) at 1 MHz, SPI mode 0. Sample once per second by default, configurable via argv[1]. Log each sample to soil_moisture.log with an ISO-8601 timestamp, the raw 10-bit ADC value, and a calculated moisture percentage (0-100%, where 0 = bone dry and 1023 = fully submerged, clamped to [0,100]). Implement robust error handling: check pigpio initialization, SPI open, every SPI transfer, and file I/O; on sensor-absent or bus-error paths, log a warning and continue. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly closes the SPI handle, flushes and closes the log file, and calls gpioTerminate() before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W to periodically read analog data from a DFRobot Soil Moisture Sensor v2.0 connected to channel 0 (ADC0) of an MCP3008 ADC via SPI, using the modern libgpiod library to access the SPI device (/dev/spidev0.0) instead of the deprecated wiringPi library. Every 5 seconds, log the raw 10-bit ADC reading and a calculated moisture percentage to the console. Assume the MCP3008 is connected to the standard hardware SPI pins (CE0 on GPIO8, MOSI on GPIO10, MISO on GPIO9, SCLK on GPIO11) with a 1 MHz clock, using 3-byte SPI transfers for the MCP3008 single-ended conversion command. Define dry and wet calibration ADC values (700 for dry, 300 for wet) and clamp the calculated moisture percentage between 0% and 100%. Implement robust error handling: check all open(), ioctl(), and read()/write() system calls, and handle SPI bus errors gracefully. Cleanly release the SPI file descriptor on program exit via signal handling (SIGINT/SIGTERM).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to periodically read pressure values from a Melexis MLX90823 analog pressure sensor, using the pigpio library. Interface the sensor's analog voltage output to the Pi via an MCP3008 10-bit ADC on the SPI0 bus (CE0 on GPIO8, MISO on GPIO9, MOSI on GPIO10, SCLK on GPIO11). Read the sensor at 1-second intervals, convert the 10-bit ADC value (0-1023) to a voltage (0-3.3V), and map the voltage to pressure in kPa assuming a 0.1 bar to 1.5 bar (10 kPa to 150 kPa) span mapped to 0.5V-4.5V. Log the readings with ISO-8601 timestamps to the console. Implement robust error handling: verify pigpio initialization, validate SPI bus reads, detect out-of-range ADC values, and handle sensor-absent conditions where the voltage is stuck at 0V or 3.3V. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the libgpiod library to periodically read analog data from a SEN0193 Capacitive Soil Moisture Sensor connected to an MCP3008 ADC over SPI. Wire the MCP3008 to SPI0 (CE0 on GPIO8, SCLK on GPIO11, MOSI on GPIO10, MISO on GPIO9), with the SEN0193 analog output connected to MCP3008 channel 0, using SPI mode 0 at 1 MHz. Read the sensor every 5 seconds, convert the 10-bit ADC value to a moisture percentage using calibration constants MIN_ADC_VALUE=300 (dry soil) and MAX_ADC_VALUE=700 (saturated soil), and log each reading to the console with a timestamp. Robustly handle errors: check all SPI open/transfer/IO operations, detect sensor-absent or bus-error paths such as the ADC value stuck at 0 or 1023 indicating a wiring fault, and cleanly release all resources, including the SPI file descriptor and GPIO lines, on all exit paths including SIGINT/SIGTERM. Do not use the deprecated wiringPi library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the spidev userspace API (/dev/spidev0.0) to read analog values from a generic soil moisture sensor (analog output) connected to an MCP3008 ADC on SPI0 CE0, channel 0. Log the moisture percentage to the console every 5 seconds. Configure SPI to mode 0, 8 bits per word, and a clock speed of 1 MHz. Use the correct 3-byte MCP3008 single-ended read command for channel 0 (start bit, config byte, don't-care byte) and extract the 10-bit result correctly. Include robust error handling for SPI open, ioctl configuration, and transfer failures. Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM cleanly to close the SPI file descriptor and exit gracefully. Clamp the moisture percentage to the 0-100 range.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 to continuously sample voltage readings from four analog sensors connected to an MCP3008 ADC via the SPI0 interface, using the libgpiod library for SPI chip-select control and standard Linux spidev for SPI communication (do not use wiringPi). Configure SPI0 (CE0 on GPIO8) at 1 MHz, Mode 0, and read channels 0 through 3 in single-ended mode using a VREF of 3.3V. Sample once per second and log timestamped voltage values to a CSV file named environmental_data.csv. Implement robust error handling for SPI communication failures, such as ioctl errors or sensor-absent/bus errors, and ensure clean resource release, closing the file, the SPI device, and the libgpiod lines, on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to read analog data from a Vegetronix VH400 soil moisture sensor connected to an MCP3008 ADC via SPI. Use SPI CE0 (bus 0, channel 0), MOSI (GPIO10), MISO (GPIO9), and SCLK (GPIO11) at a 1 MHz SPI clock speed, mode 0, reading the VH400 on MCP3008 single-ended channel 0 with a single full-duplex spiXfer call (3 bytes) per read. Activate a 12V water pump via a relay connected to GPIO17 (active-high) when the 10-bit ADC moisture reading falls below a low threshold of 300, and turn the pump off only when the reading rises above a high threshold of 600 (hysteresis). Sample every 5 seconds using a pigpio timer. Log every moisture reading and every pump state change to an in-memory circular buffer with a capacity of 20 entries, recording timestamp, moisture level, and pump state, and print the full log buffer after each sample. Implement robust error handling: check pigpio initialization, SPI open, every SPI transfer, and GPIO write, handling SPI communication failures gracefully without crashing. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, stop the timer, turn the pump off, close SPI, and terminate pigpio cleanly. Run in an infinite main loop until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to monitor a single MAX30102 pulse oximeter (SpO2/HR) connected via I2C bus 1 at address 0x57. Verify the sensor's presence by reading the Part ID register (0xFF, expected value 0x15) before proceeding. Initialize the sensor by resetting it (MODE_CONFIG register 0x06 = 0x40), clearing interrupts, configuring SpO2 mode (MODE_CONFIG = 0x03), setting SPO2_CONFIG (register 0x08) to 0x27 (100Hz, 411us pulse width, 4096 ADC range), and setting the LED pulse amplitudes (LED1_PA register 0x09 and LED2_PA register 0x0A) to 0x24. Read the FIFO data register (0x07) in 6-byte bursts (3 bytes red, 3 bytes IR) and compute SpO2 using the ratio-of-ratios method and heart rate via peak detection on the IR signal. Sample once per second, and log any SpO2 reading below 95% or heart rate reading above 100 BPM to health_log.txt with ISO 8601 timestamps. Handle I2C errors, sensor-absent conditions, and initialization failures gracefully, with error messages to stderr and the log file. Clean up all resources, including the I2C handle and pigpio, on SIGINT/SIGTERM. Use only modern pigpio APIs, no wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to read voltage values from three MCP3008 ADC channels (0, 1, 2) connected via SPI0, CE0, bus 0, at SPI mode 0 and 1 MHz. Send the MCP3008 command as a 3-byte transfer: start bit 0x01, a single-ended configuration byte with the channel selection shifted left by 4, then a dummy byte; assemble the 10-bit result from the last two bits of rx_buf[1] and all of rx_buf[2]. Calculate the voltage from the 10-bit reading using VREF = 3.3 V. Every 500 ms, log the channel number and voltage to a CSV file named 'analog_log.csv', writing a header row "Timestamp,Channel,Voltage" and appending new readings with timestamps in ISO 8601 format (YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ). Handle SPI communication errors by checking return codes and retrying or logging failures. On SIGINT (Ctrl+C), close the SPI handle, terminate pigpio, and close the CSV file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that uses the pigpio library for both SPI communication and GPIO control to read analog values from an MQ-2 gas sensor connected via an MCP3008 ADC on SPI0, CE0 on GPIO8, ADC channel 0, sampling the sensor every 500 ms, and to control an active buzzer connected to GPIO24: turn the buzzer OFF when the gas ADC value drops below a threshold of 500, and turn it back ON when the value rises to or above 500. Include robust error handling throughout: verify pigpio initialization, validate the SPI handle and every SPI read, and verify every GPIO write operation. On receiving SIGINT (Ctrl+C), close the SPI handle, reset the GPIO states, and call gpioTerminate() before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 (64-bit Bookworm, kernel 6.6+) using libgpiod to detect proximity via a GP2Y0A21YK0F Sharp IR distance sensor whose analog output is read through an ADS1115 ADC at I2C address 0x48 over /dev/i2c-1 using ioctl(I2C_SLAVE) and I2C_RDWR. Wiring: ADS1115 SDA to GPIO2, SCL to GPIO3, ADDR to GND (address 0x48), A0 to the IR sensor's analog output; a 5V relay module's IN line is on GPIO17 (active-high) and simulates a magnetic door lock release, and a magnetic reed door sensor is on GPIO27 (active-low, pulled high, LOW = door open). Use libgpiod for all digital lines. On startup, take 10 baseline samples 50 ms apart and set the trigger threshold to 80% of their average. Poll the ADC every 200 ms; if the distance reading drops below the calibrated threshold, energize the relay for 3 seconds to release the door lock, then de-energize it, then read the reed sensor and log "door opened" if LOW, otherwise "door not opened". Log every event with millisecond timestamps to /var/log/door_events.log. Check every libgpiod call, I2C ioctl, and file open; handle a sensor-absent I2C read failure by logging and continuing. On SIGINT/SIGTERM, de-energize the relay, release all libgpiod lines, close the I2C file descriptor, and exit cleanly. Do not use sysfs or wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 to log simultaneous ADC readings from three MCP3008 chips, each reading an analog soil moisture sensor on channel 0 in single-ended mode, into 'soil_moisture_log.csv' in the format timestamp,sensor1,sensor2,sensor3, logging every 5 seconds and writing the CSV header only if the file is newly created. The three MCP3008 chips share SPI0 (MOSI on GPIO10, MISO on GPIO9, SCLK on GPIO11) at 1 MHz, Mode 0 (CPOL=0, CPHA=0), with individual chip-select lines CS0 on GPIO8, CS1 on GPIO7, and CS2 on GPIO25. Use libgpiod for manual CS line control and standard Linux spidev for SPI communication; do not use wiringPi. Send the MCP3008 command as the 3-byte transfer [0x01, (0x08|channel)<<4, 0x00] and take the 10-bit result from the lower 2 bits of byte 1 and all 8 bits of byte 2. Check all return values for SPI open/ioctl, libgpiod requests, file operations, and sensor reads; if a sensor read fails, log -1 for that sensor's value. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for a graceful shutdown, releasing all resources by closing every open file descriptor and freeing all libgpiod lines and chips before the process exits.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to control a submersible 12V water pump connected via a relay to GPIO18 (active-high), triggered by a Vegetronix VH400 soil moisture sensor on channel 0 (CH0) of an MCP3008 SPI ADC, with the MCP3008 on SPI0, CE0 on GPIO8, SPI clock 1 MHz, SPI mode 0. The VH400 outputs 0-3V analog, unlike ratiometric resistive sensors, so map the 10-bit ADC value (0-1023) to a moisture percentage using experimentally determined dry=200 and wet=800 raw bounds, clamped to 0-100%. Log every moisture reading and pump activation/deactivation with timestamps to 'irrigation.log'. If moisture falls below a configurable threshold (default 30%), activate the pump for a configurable duration (default 10 s), then deactivate; check the soil every configurable interval (default 60 s). Accept command-line options -t threshold, -d duration_seconds, and -s sleep_interval. Handle SPI errors gracefully with up to 3 retries per read; if all retries fail, log the error and skip that irrigation cycle without activating the pump. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, shut off the pump, close SPI, terminate pigpio, and exit cleanly, and ensure the pump is turned off on all exit paths including SPI open failure.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to sample sound levels from an Adafruit MAX4466 electret microphone amplifier connected to channel 0 of an external MCP3008 ADC via SPI0 (CE0 on GPIO8, CLK on GPIO11, MOSI on GPIO10, MISO on GPIO9). Sample the ADC every 10 ms, maintaining an exponential moving average (EMA) of the readings, and log a detected peak whenever the raw value exceeds the EMA by a dynamic threshold margin of 20%, writing each peak to /var/log/sound_events.log with an ISO 8601 timestamp and the sampled value. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi to monitor the AIN0 analog input channel of a PCF8591 ADC at I2C address 0x48 on bus /dev/i2c-1 in a continuous loop, using libgpiod for any GPIO needs and Linux I2C via i2c-dev for bus communication (not wiringPi). Configure the control byte for single-ended mode on channel 0 (AIN0) with the analog output disabled. Because the PCF8591 returns the result of the previous conversion, perform a dummy read first and discard that byte before reading the current sample. Sample every 100 ms and print each sample value (0-255) to stdout. Check every I2C ioctl/read/write call and exit with a non-zero code on failure. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl-C) cleanly by closing the I2C file descriptor before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to monitor a Honeywell SS49E linear Hall-effect sensor. The SS49E is an analog sensor powered from the 3.3 V rail, so sample its voltage output at 1 Hz via an ADS1115 ADC on I2C bus 1 at address 0x48, single-ended channel AIN0. Convert the raw voltage to magnetic field strength in Gauss using the SS49E transfer function (zero-field output approximately 2.5 V, sensitivity approximately 1.4 mV/Gauss, Vcc = 3.3 V), and store the last 10 readings in a circular buffer. If the rolling average of the buffer exceeds a compile-time threshold (e.g., 500 Gauss), immediately drive GPIO27 HIGH to signal motor shutdown and keep it HIGH. Log all readings, threshold events, and errors via syslog. Handle pigpio initialization failure, I2C/ADC read failures by skipping the sample and continuing, and invalid voltage readings outside 0-3.3 V. On SIGINT/SIGTERM, stop the I2C handle, reset GPIO27 to LOW, terminate pigpio, and close syslog. Do not use wiringPi, and do not include MQTT or networking code.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to read soil moisture from a Vegetronix VH400 sensor whose analog output is connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC via SPI0 CE0 at 1 MHz, SPI mode 0. Activate a 12V submersible water pump connected to GPIO18 via a relay when the 10-bit ADC reading drops below a threshold of 300, running the pump for 10 seconds per watering cycle, then reading again every 60 seconds. Log timestamps and moisture levels to 'watering_events.txt'. Implement robust SPI communication error handling by validating the channel, checking the spiXfer return value, and detecting stuck or invalid ADC values, plus graceful GPIO initialization failure recovery. Ensure the pump is deactivated immediately on any error or shutdown path, with clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to read analog values from a YL-83 rain sensor whose analog output is wired to channel 0 (CH0) of an MCP3008 ADC on SPI0 (CE0, bus 0), with the MCP3008 VDD at 3.3 V so ADC full-scale = 1023, read in single-ended mode. Use SPI mode 0 at 1 MHz. Sample once per second and map the 10-bit ADC value (0-1023) to a rainfall intensity level of 0-10, where 0 is dry and 10 is heavily raining. Log each reading to stdout with a timestamp, the raw ADC value, and the intensity level. Check pigpio initialization, the SPI open, and every spiXfer call; on SPI transfer failure, print an error and retry on the next cycle rather than continuing with stale data. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) for graceful shutdown by closing the SPI handle and terminating pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that uses the pigpio library to read a potentiometer connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC (SPI0, CE0 on GPIO8) and uses the 10-bit reading to control the duty cycle of a PWM motor on GPIO18. Configure SPI at 1 MHz, mode 0, and PWM at 1 kHz with a range of 0-1023 so the ADC value maps directly to the duty cycle. Continuously read the ADC and update the PWM every 100 ms, printing both values to stdout. Access the BH1750 at I2C address 0x23 on /dev/i2c-1 using continuous high-resolution mode 2 (command 0x11), waiting 180 ms before reading the 2-byte result. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to monitor an MQ-135 air quality sensor (analog output) via an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (channel 0, 1 MHz, mode 0), reading MCP3008 channel 0 (single-ended) every 5 seconds. Convert the ADC value (0-1023) to an AQI using a linear mapping (0-500). Control a 12V ventilation fan connected to GPIO18 (BCM) via a relay: turn it on when AQI > 100, off otherwise. Log the timestamp and AQI to 'air_quality.log' in append mode. Use the proper MCP3008 SPI protocol: start bit (0x01), single-ended mode (0x08), channel select (0x00-0x07), then read the 10-bit result from response bytes 1 and 2. Implement robust error handling for SPI communication failures, including retry logic and re-initialization: on SPI read failure, retry up to 3 times with a 1-second delay; if still failing, re-initialize SPI and continue. Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM for graceful shutdown (fan off, close SPI, close log, terminate pigpio), and ensure all resources are released on exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the libgpiod library (not bcm2835 or wiringPi) for any GPIO control and standard Linux spidev for SPI communication with an MCP3008 ADC, to read analog voltage from an MQ-3 alcohol sensor connected to MCP3008 channel 0 via SPI0 (CE0 on GPIO8), channel 0 single-ended mode, 1 MHz SPI clock, SPI mode 0, 8 bits per word. Sample every 1 second with ISO 8601 UTC timestamps and log readings to 'alcohol_log.txt'. Send the MCP3008 command as tx[0]=0x01 (start), tx[1]=(channel<<4)|0x80 (single-ended + channel), tx[2]=0x00, and compute result = ((rx[1] & 0x03) << 8) | rx[2]. Convert ADC values (0-1023) to approximate PPM using PPM = (adc_value * 0.5) - 10.0. Classify readings: above 50 PPM as 'Alcohol detected! Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the libgpiod library, together with the standard Linux spidev SPI interface, to read analog soil moisture data from a Vegetronix VH400 sensor via an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (CE0, SCLK=GPIO11, MOSI=GPIO10, MISO=GPIO9), configured for single-ended mode on channel 0. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads analog voltage from a DRV5055-A1 Hall-effect sensor via an external MCP3008 ADC over SPI, using the Linux spidev interface on /dev/spidev0.0 at 1 MHz, SPI mode 0, 8 bits per word, together with libgpiod (gpiochip0, line 8) to manually drive chip-select low during each SPI transfer and high afterward. Hardware wiring: MCP3008 VDD and VREF tied to the Pi's 3.3 V rail; MCP3008 DOUT to GPIO 10, DIN to GPIO 9, CLK to GPIO 11, and CS/SHDN to GPIO 8; DRV5055-A1 VOUT to MCP3008 channel 0, DRV5055 VCC to 3.3 V. The MCP3008 is a 10-bit ADC (0-1023) with VREF = 3.3 V, so compute Vout_mV = adc_value * 3300 / 1023. Sample every 500 ms and append a CSV row to "magnetic_log.txt" as <unix_epoch>,<B_mt_two_decimals>. Check every open, ioctl, SPI transfer, fopen, and fprintf call and propagate errors; if an ADC read fails, log the error to stderr, skip that sample, and continue the loop. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library that reads analog voltage from a TI DRV5055VA Hall-effect sensor via an external MCP3008 ADC over SPI0 (CE0, GPIO 8, 9, 10, 11), with the sensor output wired to MCP3008 channel 0 (single-ended) and the sensor powered at 3.3 V. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to monitor soil moisture with a DFRobot resistive soil moisture sensor connected to an MCP3008 ADC over SPI channel 0 (CE0, mode 0, 1 MHz), with the sensor's analog output wired to MCP3008 single-ended input channel 0. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to read current from a Melexis MLX91211 analog-output current sensor via an MCP3008 SPI ADC. Use libgpiod (v2) for GPIO input and invoke the libcamera-still CLI utility for image capture. Open the GPIO chip and claim GPIO17 as input with edge-falling or edge-rising detection, applying a 50 ms debounce via a falling-edge wait with timeout. On motion detection, generate a timestamped filename in the format YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS_mmm.jpg and run libcamera-still with "-o <filename> --width 640 --height 480 -q 85 --timeout 2000 --nopreview" (assume the images directory already exists), checking its return code and logging failures. Log all events, with timestamps, to /home/pi/motion_capture.log. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM cleanly by releasing all libgpiod resources and closing file descriptors. Do not use wiringPi, and do not use ZeroMQ or any network publishing — save to the local file system only.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi (32-bit or 64-bit) that captures a single frame from a USB UVC camera at /dev/video0 using the V4L2 API, crops a specific region, and saves the result as a raw YUYV file — V4L2 only, no libgpiod, pigpio, or wiringPi. Open /dev/video0 read/write and verify it is a V4L2 video capture device via VIDIOC_QUERYCAP. Negotiate format 640x480, V4L2_PIX_FMT_YUYV, V4L2_FIELD_NONE, and use memory-mapped streaming with one buffer (VIDIOC_REQBUFS, VIDIOC_QUERYBUF, mmap, VIDIOC_QBUF). Start streaming, then use select() with a 2-second timeout to wait for the frame, handling EINTR retries in ioctl calls. Dequeue the buffer and verify the captured width, height, and pixel format match the requested values before processing. Crop the region starting at (100, 50) with size 200x150 from the YUYV frame, copying complete 4-byte YUYV macroblocks (Y0, U, Y1, V) to avoid color corruption, and save the cropped frame to cropped.yuv (200*150*2 bytes). Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so Ctrl-C cleanly stops streaming, munmaps buffers, closes the fd, and frees memory. Check every syscall, ioctl, mmap, fopen, and fwrite return value, printing errno via perror on failure and exiting with EXIT_FAILURE.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to control two SG90 servo motors connected to GPIO17 (pan) and GPIO18 (tilt), forming a basic pan-tilt camera mount. Read user input from stdin — arrow keys for up, down, left, right — to adjust pan and tilt angles in 5-degree increments, enforcing limits of 0 to 180 degrees, with initial angles of 90 degrees (neutral). Use pigpio's hardware PWM at 50 Hz, with pulse widths ranging from 500 microseconds (0 degrees) to 2500 microseconds (180 degrees). Handle pigpio initialization failure gracefully by printing an error and exiting with code 1. On SIGINT (Ctrl+C) or a 'q' input, set both servos to the neutral position and terminate pigpio cleanly. Validate all angle inputs and PWM settings, printing clear error messages for out-of-range angles or PWM failures. Include a 100 ms delay between commands to prevent excessive CPU usage. Use only pigpio functions — not wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that displays real-time CPU temperature, read from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp, and CPU usage percentage, computed from /proc/stat, on a 128x64 I2C OLED screen using the SSD1306 driver. Use the pigpio library for I2C communication on bus 1, addressing the SSD1306 at 0x3C. Implement a basic 5x7 bitmap font to render the temperature and usage text on the display, updating the display once per second. Handle file read errors by returning specific error strings to the display instead of the missing values, and handle I2C communication failures by logging a message to stderr and exiting gracefully, checking every I2C write operation for an error return. Include signal handling for SIGINT so that all resources are released cleanly on exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B, using the pigpio library, that reads pulses from a YF-S201 water flow sensor connected to GPIO17 and calculates the flow rate in liters per minute using the sensor's calibration figure of approximately 450 pulses per liter. Log the current flow rate and the running total volume to the console every 1 second, with robust error handling for GPIO initialization failures. Every 10 seconds, also update a small HD44780 LCD screen connected via I2C (bus 1, address 0x27) to display the current flow rate together with the accumulated volume, using pigpio's I2C functions and handling any I2C communication errors that occur. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for a graceful shutdown that releases all GPIO and I2C resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library exclusively (no wiringPi) to display real-time wind speed and direction on a 16x2 LCD (PCF8574 I2C backpack at address 0x27, bus 1), updating every 500 ms. Count anemometer pulses on GPIO17 via a rising-edge interrupt, computing wind speed as pulses multiplied by 0.5 m/s per pulse, accumulated over each 500 ms sample window. Read the wind vane from channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC over SPI0/CE0, mode 0, 1 MHz, linearly mapping the 10-bit ADC value (0-1023) to 0-359 degrees. Check every pigpio, I2C, and SPI call; detect sensor-absent conditions such as an ADC reading stuck at 0 or 1023, or I2C/SPI failures, and print diagnostic messages to stderr while continuing to run. Use pigpio's I2C and SPI bit-bang helpers (bbI2COpen/bbSPIOpen) or direct /dev/i2c and /dev/spidev access via pigpio's spi0SPIOpen/i2cOpen where appropriate. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, releasing all resources — the SPI handle, the I2C handle, and pigpio.

prompt: Write a C program using the libgpiod library for a Raspberry Pi to create a wave-like animation on an 8x8 common-anode LED matrix. The matrix rows are anodes, connected via GPIO to +3.3V, and columns are cathodes, connected via GPIO to ground: rows on GPIO17, 18, 27, 22, 23, 24, 25, 4 (BCM numbering), columns on GPIO5, 6, 12, 13, 19, 16, 26, 20. Implement a scanning display function that lights one row at a time — row HIGH and column LOW lights an LED (common-anode logic) — using a scan delay of 800 microseconds per row. Create two wave patterns, left-to-right and right-to-left, that shift each frame. Check all libgpiod calls, printing descriptive error messages to stderr and exiting with a non-zero code on failure. Handle graceful shutdown on SIGINT by releasing GPIO lines and cleaning up. Do not use wiringPi or any deprecated library.

Write a C program using the libgpiod v2 API (gpiod_chip_open, gpiod_line_request_output, etc.) for a Raspberry Pi to create a wave-like animation on an 8x8 common-anode LED matrix with 8 row anodes and 8 column cathodes. Wire row pins GPIO2, 3, 4, 17, 27, 22, 10, 9 to the row anodes, and column pins GPIO14, 15, 18, 23, 24, 25, 8, 7 to the column cathodes through current-limiting resistors (e.g. 220 ohm). prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 to interface with an E18-D50NK IR proximity sensor via GPIO using the libgpiod library. The E18-D50NK outputs LOW when an object is detected within its calibrated range of 10-30 cm, and HIGH otherwise. Use GPIO line 4 (physical pin 7) for the sensor input and GPIO line 17 (physical pin 11) for an LED output, polling every 100 ms. When an object is detected (sensor reads LOW), blink the LED for 100 ms (ON then OFF) and log a timestamped event to "proximity.log" in ISO 8601 UTC format, e.g. "2024-01-15T12:34:56Z Object detected" — log only on the falling edge (HIGH to LOW transition, object entering range) to avoid duplicate entries while the object remains in range. Open the GPIO chip by name "gpiochip4" (the Raspberry Pi 5 default); if that fails, fall back to gpiod_chip_open_by_name("gpiochip0") — do not use gpiod_chip_open_lookup without arguments. Check all libgpiod calls and handle file I/O errors, ensuring clean resource release — releasing GPIO lines and closing the chip — on all exit paths, including SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library over I2C bus 1 (default address 0x60) to read proximity (PS1) and ambient light (ALS_VIS) data from a Silicon Labs Si1145 sensor. On startup verify the PART_ID register (0x00) returns 0x45, then write 0x17 to HW_KEY (0x07), set CH_LIST (0x4F) to enable the PS1 and ALS_VIS channels, configure the measurement rates, and use the COMMAND register (0x30) with 0x06 (ALS_FORCE) and 0x07 (PS_FORCE) to trigger measurements. Read PS1 data from registers 0x18-0x19 and ALS_VIS data from registers 0x22-0x23, little-endian. Check every I2C read/write return code and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths gracefully. Once per second, in an infinite loop, log each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp, proximity value, and ambient light value to a CSV file named 'biometric_data.log', flushing the file after every write. Install a SIGINT handler that closes the I2C handle, closes the log file, and calls gpioTerminate() for clean shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the libgpiod library to drive an HC-SR04 ultrasonic distance sensor for a proximity-based plant watering reminder. Use TRIGGER on GPIO 17 (BCM, output) and ECHO on GPIO 27 (BCM, input). Because the HC-SR04 echo pin outputs 5V logic and the Pi's GPIO is only 3.3V-tolerant, use a voltage divider (e.g. 1kOhm/2kOhm) on the echo line to protect the input. Generate a 10 microsecond trigger pulse, measure the echo pulse width using libgpiod edge events with CLOCK_MONOTONIC, and compute distance as (pulse_seconds * 34300) / 2 cm. Check every libgpiod call, apply a 30 ms timeout on each phase, treat an echo that never rises as sensor-absent and an echo stuck high as a timeout, and reject readings outside 2-400 cm. Log every measurement, including error and timeout entries, with an ISO-8601 timestamp to 'distance_log.txt', polling every 60 seconds. If the measured distance is below 15 cm, log a 'Time to water the plant!' reminder. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, releasing all libgpiod resources and closing the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to continuously read an Adafruit APDS9960 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x39. On startup verify the sensor ID register (0x92) equals 0xAB, then configure ENABLE (0x80) to 0x03, ATIME (0x81) to 0xDB, WTIME (0x83) to 0xF6, PPULSE (0x8E) to 0x87, CONTROL (0xF1) to 0x03, and CONFIG2 (0x90) to 0x01. Every 100 ms read the 16-bit raw RGB color values from registers 0x96-0x9B and the 8-bit proximity value from register 0x9C, logging both with a timestamp to a CSV file named 'color_proximity_log.csv' only when proximity exceeds a threshold of 200. On I2C communication errors, re-open the bus and re-initialize the sensor rather than aborting. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle and the CSV file and releasing all pigpio resources. On any I2C communication error, close and reopen the I2C bus and fully re-initialize the sensor's configuration registers before resuming, rather than aborting the program.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface to interface with a Silicon Labs Si1182-A-GMR optical sensor and measure heart rate. Open /dev/i2c-1, set the 7-bit slave address 0x5A via ioctl(I2C_SLAVE), and perform register reads and writes with i2c_smbus_* helpers, checking every return code and aborting on error. On startup, read the PART_ID register (0x00) and verify it returns the expected Si1182 part identifier; if the read fails or the ID mismatches, print a diagnostic and exit non-zero. Configure continuous proximity measurement by writing the MEAS_RATE0 register (0x08) with an appropriate rate value, then issue a reset/start command via the COMMAND register (0x47). Every 100 ms, read the 16-bit proximity data registers PS_DATA0 (0x24) and PS_DATA1 (0x25), combine them little-endian, and compute a placeholder BPM from the proximity signal. Log each sample as 'timestamp,bpm' with an ISO-8601 timestamp to 'heartrate.csv', calling fflush after every write. If an I2C read fails mid-loop, print a warning to stderr, skip that sample, and continue rather than crash. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that sets a volatile running=false flag so the loop exits cleanly, then closes the I2C file descriptor, closes the CSV file, and returns 0.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to interface with an Adafruit VL53L0X Time-of-Flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x29; do not use wiringPi. Configure GPIO 17 (BCM numbering) with a pull-up and trigger a single distance measurement on each falling edge detected there. Verify sensor presence at 0x29 before initialization. To range, write 0x01 to SYSRANGE_START (register 0x00), poll bit 0 of RESULT_INTERRUPT_STATUS (register 0x13) until it sets, with a timeout of about 100 ms, then read the 14-byte result block starting at RESULT_RANGE_STATUS (register 0x14) and extract the 16-bit distance from bytes 10-11, and finally clear the interrupt by writing 0x01 to SYSTEM_INTERRUPT_CLEAR (register 0x0B). Apply robust error handling to every I2C transaction and to sensor-absent and timeout paths. Log each timestamped distance measurement, in millimetres, to 'distance_log.txt' in CSV format as 'timestamp,distance_mm'. Handle SIGINT for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle and log file and releasing pigpio resources on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library over I2C bus 1 to measure distance with a TDK CH101 ultrasonic sensor at its default address 0x45. Trigger a measurement, wait about 50 ms, then read the 16-bit distance result in millimetres. Sample every 200 ms, logging each reading as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, <distance_mm>' to 'distance_log.txt' and also printing it to stdout. Use a fixed-size local buffer for the timestamp so no malloc/free happens per iteration. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl-C) gracefully by stopping the loop and closing the I2C handle, log file, and pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with two TCRT5000 IR reflective sensors on GPIO 17 and GPIO 18 (BCM numbering) to detect object proximity. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to interface with a Silicon Labs Si1182-GMR Optical Proximity and Ambient Light Sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x60. Continuously read distance measurements every 50 ms, logging each reading with a timestamp to 'tof_log.txt', and turn on an LED connected to GPIO 17 whenever the measured distance falls below a configurable threshold, default 100 mm, passed as the first command-line argument. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface (open/ioctl/read/write on /dev/i2c-1) to interface with an Omron B5L-LD50-07050 3D TOF sensor at its default 7-bit address 0x50; do not use wiringPi. To request a distance measurement, write the 4-byte command frame {0x50, 0x0A, 0x00, 0x01} to the sensor, wait at least 10 ms, then read a 15-byte response frame, validating that byte 0 of the header equals 0x50. Use /dev/i2c-1 and standard open(2), ioctl(I2C_SLAVE), read(2), and write(2) system calls, and implement a helper that performs an I2C register read using a combined write-then-read transaction. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to interface with a VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x29. Verify the sensor model ID equals 0xEA at register 0x010F during initialization, perform a software reset by writing 0x00 then 0x01 to register 0x0000, configure the sensor for a 50 ms timing budget, and start ranging by writing 0x01 to register 0x0080. Every 50 ms, poll the data-ready bit (bit 0 of register 0x0089) before reading the 16-bit distance from registers 0x0096-0x0097, and activate a buzzer connected to GPIO23 if the measured distance falls below 100mm. Handle all I2C read/write errors gracefully, with robust error handling for I2C communication failures and sensor absence. Log distance readings using a POSIX message queue. Ensure clean resource release of the I2C handle, message queue, GPIO, and pigpio on SIGINT. Structure the initialization sequence so that the model-ID check, the software reset, and the timing-budget configuration all complete successfully before ranging begins, and treat a failure at any of these steps as a fatal startup error.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to implement an interrupt-driven parking sensor with a single HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor on GPIO 17 (trigger, BCM) and GPIO 27 (echo, BCM), with a buzzer on GPIO 22 (BCM). Send a 10 microsecond HIGH trigger pulse and use gpioSetAlertFuncEx for interrupt-driven measurement of the echo pulse width, computing distance using a speed of sound of 34300 cm/s divided by 2 for the round trip, and handling pigpio's 32-bit tick wraparound correctly. Valid readings range from 2 cm to 400 cm. Display the distance in centimeters on the console every 100 ms. Activate the buzzer continuously while the distance is less than 30 cm, and turn it off once the distance returns to 30 cm or above. Check pigpio initialization, GPIO mode configuration, and alert registration for errors, and detect and clearly report sensor-absent (timeout/no echo) and invalid reading (out-of-range) conditions. Perform a clean shutdown on SIGINT that turns off the buzzer and calls gpioTerminate().

Automatically open the gate when an object is detected within 20 cm and close it when the path is clear. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library's I2C functions (gpioInitialise, i2cOpen, i2cWriteByteData, i2cReadByteData, i2cClose, gpioTerminate) to continuously read proximity data from a Silicon Labs Si1145 sensor at I2C address 0x60. Initialise the sensor with the following write sequence: 0x03 to register 0x07 (hardware key), 0x02 to register 0x06 (MEAS_RATE, 2 ms), 0x00 to register 0x1A (no interrupt), 0x0B to register 0x21 (ALS_VIS_IR_ADC_COUNTER), 0x00 to register 0x24 (ALS_VIS_ADC_GAIN), 0x49 to register 0x22 (PS_ADC_COUNTER, 16-bit, 1/15 gain), 0x03 to register 0x0C (PS_LED21, 180 mA), 0x0F to register 0x0F (PS_LED3, 180 mA), 0x03 to register 0x11 (PS_ADC_MISC, small IR), 0x07 to register 0x0D (PS_ADC_GAIN, 7.7x), and 0x03 to register 0x80 (COMMAND, PS_FORCE). After initialisation, continuously read the proximity value from registers 0x16 (PS1_DATA0, low byte) and 0x17 (PS1_DATA1, high byte), combining them into a 16-bit unsigned integer, and append each reading with a timestamp (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS) to 'proximity_log.txt'. Check every I2C write/read operation for errors; on a communication failure, log the error together with a timestamp and retry up to 3 times before exiting, and handle sensor initialisation failures by reporting a clear, specific error message rather than failing silently. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers for a clean shutdown that closes the I2C handle, closes the log file, and terminates pigpio. The program should run indefinitely, taking one reading per cycle, until it is interrupted by the user.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to measure distance with an interrupt-driven HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor (trigger on GPIO17, echo on GPIO18) and activate a buzzer on GPIO27 when the distance falls below 20 cm. Configure the trigger pin as output, the echo pin as input with a falling/rising edge alert callback, and the buzzer pin as output. Generate a 10 us trigger pulse on GPIO17, then measure the echo pulse width using an interrupt handler that records the rising and falling edge timestamps, computing distance in cm as round-trip time * 0.0343 / 2 (speed of sound = 0.0343 cm/us). Print the distance to stdout every second; if the distance is below 20 cm set the buzzer pin high, otherwise set it low. Initialise pigpio and check for errors, exiting with a clear message if initialisation fails; check all pigpio calls (gpioSetMode, gpioSetAlertFuncEx, gpioWrite, gpioDelay) and print errors to stderr if they fail. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) by terminating pigpio and exiting, with proper resource cleanup on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to implement a parking assist system with an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor (trigger on GPIO4, echo on GPIO17) and an SG90 servo motor (signal on GPIO18). Measure distance and display it in centimeters on the console, and rotate the servo proportionally to distance: 0 degrees (500 us pulse) at 200 cm, 90 degrees (1500 us pulse) at 110 cm, and 180 degrees (2500 us pulse) at 20 cm. Use gpioDelay for timing rather than busy-wait loops. Check pigpio initialisation, handle echo timeout by returning -1.0, and retry on sensor errors. Update the distance reading and servo angle every 100 ms, running continuously until interrupted. Handle SIGINT with a graceful cleanup: stop the servo, terminate pigpio, and exit cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to interface with a VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x29 and control a servo-actuated gate on GPIO18 (hardware PWM-capable). Initialise the sensor by verifying the model ID 0xEA at register 0x010F, setting the timing budget, and starting ranging, then poll distance from the correct 16-bit distance register. Open the gate when an object is detected closer than 200 mm and close it when the object moves beyond 250 mm (hysteresis), smoothly transitioning the servo between 1000 us (closed) and 2000 us (open) pulse widths. Log every open/close event with a timestamp to 'gate_log.txt'. Handle I2C read/write errors gracefully, and ensure clean release of the I2C handle, pigpio, and log file on SIGINT.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to implement a parking assist system with an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor (trigger on GPIO23, echo on GPIO24, measuring 2 cm to 400 cm) and an SG90 micro servo (signal on GPIO18, powered from 5V with a common ground) that visually indicates distance by rotating from 0 degrees (closest) to 180 degrees (farthest). Use a 10 us trigger pulse (not 10 ms), and measure the echo pulse width with microsecond precision using gpioTick(), applying a 50 ms (50000 us) timeout on both the rising and falling edges and returning -1.0 on timeout. Compute distance as (pulse_duration_us * 0.0343) / 2 (speed of sound 343 m/s). Map distances below 20 cm to 0 degrees, above 200 cm to 180 degrees, and values in between linearly, controlling the servo via gpioServo() with pulse widths of 500 us for 0 degrees and 2500 us for 180 degrees. Print distance and angle each cycle, with a 100 ms delay between measurements. Initialise pigpio with error checking, exiting with a clear message on failure; check every pigpio call, handle sensor timeout, and avoid division by zero or invalid angles. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) by stopping the servo (gpioServo with 0) and terminating pigpio cleanly. Use only pigpio, not wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with a Silicon Labs Si7005 I2C humidity and temperature sensor at I2C bus 1, address 0x40, logging readings to the console every 2 seconds. Write 0x00 to the CONFIG register (0x03) to select the internal temperature sensor and disable the heater, waiting 10 ms afterward. After writing the register address to read, wait 10 ms for conversion, then read the temperature register (0x01) and the humidity register (0x02). Convert readings using T = (175.72 * raw) / 65536.0 - 46.85 and H = (125.0 * raw) / 65536.0 - 6.0. Verify pigpio initialisation, the I2C bus open, and every I2C read/write operation; if a transaction fails, close and re-open the I2C handle to attempt recovery. Handle SIGINT for a graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle and terminating pigpio on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to periodically read raw accelerometer and gyroscope data from a TDK InvenSense MPU-6050 over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x68 (SDA on GPIO2, SCL on GPIO3), logging it to the console. Initialise pigpio and verify the sensor is present by reading the WHO_AM_I register (expect 0x68). Reset the device via PWR_MGMT_1 (0x6B), wait for it to stabilize, then clear the sleep bit. Set the sample-rate divider (0x19) to 7 for 125 Hz output, and configure ACCEL_CONFIG (0x1C) for a ±2 g range and GYRO_CONFIG (0x1B) for a ±250 deg/s range. Every 100 ms, read the 14-byte data block starting at register 0x3B (accelerometer XYZ, temperature, gyroscope XYZ) using i2cReadI2CBlockData, parse the big-endian int16 values, and print them to stdout. Handle I2C read/write errors and sensor-absent conditions without terminating the loop unexpectedly. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by closing the I2C handle and calling gpioTerminate() before exiting, and print a brief startup message when the program begins along with a clean-shutdown message when it terminates.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to periodically read temperature and humidity from an Adafruit SHT40 I2C sensor connected to I2C bus 1 at address 0x44, logging readings to the console every 5 seconds. To trigger a high-repeatability measurement, send command 0xFD, wait at least 10 ms, then read 6 bytes: 2 bytes temperature, 1 CRC byte, 2 bytes humidity, 1 CRC byte. Validate both CRC-8 checksums (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF). Convert raw values using T = -45 + 175 * raw / 65535 and RH = -6 + 125 * raw / 65535, clamped to 0-100%. On any I2C read/write error or CRC failure, print a diagnostic message to stderr and re-open the I2C bus before the next attempt. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for a graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle and terminating pigpio on exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the Linux I2C character device interface via /dev/i2c-1 to read ambient and object temperatures from a Melexis MLX90614ESF-BAA infrared temperature sensor at its default address 0x5A, for a contactless food safety monitoring system. Read ambient temperature from register 0x06 and object temperature from register 0x07 every 5 seconds. Log each timestamped reading to a comma-separated file named 'temperature_log.csv'. Handle I2C initialisation failures, sensor-absent scenarios (read errors), and file I/O errors gracefully rather than terminating unexpectedly. Handle SIGINT for clean resource release, closing both the I2C file descriptor and the log file before the process exits.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to periodically sample temperature from a Sensirion STS30-DIS sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x4A. The STS30-DIS is a temperature-only sensor with no humidity output, so only temperature is sampled, once every 5 seconds, and logged together with a timestamp to a file named 'enclosure_temp_log.txt' that the program keeps open across the run. Implement robust error handling for I2C communication failures, including sensor-absent and bus-error paths, logging any errors that occur to a separate file, 'error_log.txt'. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including proper signal handling for Ctrl+C.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to interface with a Sensirion SDP810-125Pa differential pressure sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x25, simulating a simple ventilation system monitoring application. Configure the sensor for continuous measurement by sending command bytes 0x36 0x08, wait at least 1 ms, then read the 9-byte data frame containing differential pressure (2 bytes + CRC), temperature (2 bytes + CRC), and scale factors (2 bytes + CRC), converting the raw pressure and temperature using their respective scale factors. Poll the sensor every 1 second, and log the ISO 8601 UTC timestamp, differential pressure in Pa, and temperature in °C to a comma-separated file named 'pressure_log.csv', writing a header row if the file is new. Check all pigpio and file I/O operations, validate the CRC-8 checksum for every reading (polynomial 0x31, initialization 0xFF), and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths gracefully. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses standard Linux I2C ioctls on /dev/i2c-1 to interface with a Sensirion SHT40 humidity and temperature sensor on I2C bus 1 (SDA on GPIO2, SCL on GPIO3) at the 7-bit address 0x44, simulating a smart greenhouse environment monitor. Use the high-repeatability measurement command 0xFD, which returns 6 bytes: 2 bytes temperature MSB+LSB, 1 CRC byte, 2 bytes humidity MSB+LSB, 1 CRC byte; wait at least 10 ms for the measurement to complete before reading. Robustly handle I2C open, ioctl, write, and read errors; if the sensor is absent or a read fails, log an error and retry on the next cycle. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (gpioInitialise/gpioTerminate, i2cOpen/i2cClose, i2cWriteDevice/i2cReadDevice) to periodically read differential pressure and temperature from a Sensirion SDP31 (±500 Pa) sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x28. Send the continuous measurement trigger command 0x21 0x96, wait at least 1 ms, then read 6 bytes (pressure MSB, pressure LSB, CRC, temperature MSB, temperature LSB, CRC). Convert raw pressure to Pa as raw_pressure / 60.0 and raw temperature to °C as raw_temperature / 200.0. Sample every 100 ms, logging each sample as timestamp,pressure_pa,temperature_c to a comma-separated file named 'airflow.log', flushing after each write. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read temperature and humidity from a Sensirion SHT35-DIS-B sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x44, simulating a greenhouse environment monitor. Use the high-repeatability, clock-stretching-disabled measurement command (0x24, 0x00) and wait at least 15 ms before reading the 6-byte result. Validate the 8-bit CRC for both the temperature and humidity words; if the CRC fails or the I2C read/write fails, retry up to 3 times with a 1-second delay, and if all retries fail, log NaN values. Convert raw values to degrees Celsius and %RH using the standard Sensirion formulas, then add a simulated sinusoidal offset (±2 °C, ±5 %RH) over a 1-hour period to the actual readings. Log data in ISO-8601 UTC format to 'environmental_data.txt' every 5 seconds. Implement robust error handling for pigpio initialisation, I2C open/read/write, and file open. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and terminating pigpio cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the standard Linux I2C i2c-dev interface to interface with a Sensirion SDP810-125Pa differential pressure sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x25. Send the continuous measurement command (0x362F), wait for the conversion time of approximately 45 ms, and read 9 bytes containing pressure, temperature, and scale factor, each with an 8-bit CRC. Validate the CRC-8 checksums (polynomial 0x31, initial 0xFF) and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths. Convert the raw data to pressure in Pa and temperature in °C using the correct formulas. Log the timestamp, pressure, and temperature to a CSV file named 'airflow.csv' every 1 second. Implement graceful shutdown on SIGINT and SIGTERM, ensuring the I2C file descriptor and any open file handles are properly closed.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to read temperature and humidity from a Sensirion SHT35-DIS-B sensor connected to I2C bus 1 at address 0x44 (ADDR pin tied to GND). Use the single-shot high-repeatability clock-stretching-disabled measurement command (0x2400); after sending it, wait at least 15 ms before reading 6 bytes (temperature MSB, temperature LSB, temperature CRC, humidity MSB, humidity LSB, humidity CRC), validating both CRC-8 checksums (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF). Convert raw values using T = -45 + 175 * raw / 65535 and RH = 100 * raw / 65535. Log each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp to a CSV file named 'environment.csv' (columns: timestamp,temperature_c,humidity_pct), writing a header row if the file does not already exist or is empty, sampling every 5 seconds. Check pigpio initialisation, I2C open, every I2C read/write, CRC validation, and file open; on failure print a descriptive error to stderr and continue or exit appropriately. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler for clean shutdown that closes the I2C handle and calls gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface (open(), ioctl(), read(), write()) to periodically read temperature and humidity from an Adafruit Si7021 sensor at I2C address 0x40 on bus 1 (GPIO 2/3), simulating a greenhouse monitoring system. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to read differential pressure from a Honeywell Zephyr HAF Series HAFBLF0100A2AX5 digital airflow sensor over I2C bus 1 at 7-bit address 0x28, and drives a PWM fan on GPIO18 (a hardware-PWM-capable pin) at 25 kHz based on the computed flow rate. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to read an STLM75 digital temperature sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x48, reading temperature register 0x00 once per second. The STLM75 returns a 16-bit two's-complement word with 9-bit resolution (sign bit, 8 data bits, and the low 7 bits always 0); because pigpio's i2cReadWordData returns bytes in little-endian order, swap the two bytes before extracting the value, then right-shift by 7 and divide by 2 to get degrees Celsius. Store each reading in a 10-element circular buffer in memory and compute the running average. Turn on an LED on GPIO 17 when the average temperature exceeds 28.0 °C and turn it off otherwise. Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (gpioInitialise, i2cOpen, i2cClose, i2cReadDevice, i2cWriteDevice, gpioTerminate) to interface with a Sensirion SCD30 CO2 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x61. int main() {
    int i;
    int i2c_handle;
    FILE *file;
    float temperature;
    struct pigpio *gpio;
    struct pigpio_config config;

    // Initialize pigpio
    gpio = pigpio_init();
    if (gpio == NULL) {
        printf("Failed to initialize pigpio\n");
        return 1;
    }

    // Set up I2C configuration
    config.gpio_i2c_sda = 5;
    config.gpio_i2c_scl = 6;
    config.gpio_i2c_sda_pull = PI_GPIO_PULL_UP;
    config.gpio_i2c_scl_pull = PI_GPIO_PULL_UP;
    config.gpio_i2c_sda_edge = PI_GPIO_EDGE_RISING;
    config.gpio_i2c_scl_edge = PI_GPIO_EDGE_RISING;
    config.gpio_i2c_speed = PI_I2C_SPEED_100KHZ;

    // Initialize I2C
    i2c_handle = pigpio_i2c_open(&config);
    if (i2c_handle == -1) {
        printf("Failed to open I2C\n");
        pigpio_exit(gpio);
        return 1;
    }

    // Check device ID
    uint8_t device_id[3];
    if (pigpio_i2c_read(i2c_handle, I2C_ADDRESS, I2C_REG_DEVICE_ID, device_id, 3) != 3) {
        printf("Failed to read device ID\n");
        pigpio_i2c_close(i2c_handle);
        pigpio_exit(gpio);
        return 1;
    }
    if (memcmp(device_id, "0117", 3) != 0) {
        printf("Device ID mismatch\n");
        pigpio_i2c_close(i2c_handle);
        pigpio_exit(gpio);
        return 1;
    }

    // Open file for writing
    file = fopen("greenhouse_temps.dat", "wb");
    if (file == NULL) {
        printf("Failed to open file\n");
        pigpio_i2c_close(i2c_handle);
        pigpio_exit(gpio);
        return 1;
    }

    // Main loop
    while (1) {
        // Read temperature
        temperature = 0.0;
        if (pigpio_i2c_read(i2c_handle, I2C_ADDRESS, I2C_REG_TEMPERATURE, &temperature, 2) != 2) {
            printf("Failed to read temperature\n");
            break;
        }

        // Convert temperature to float
        temperature = (temperature * 0.0078125);

        // Write temperature to file
        fwrite(&temperature, sizeof(float), 1, file);

        // Sleep for 60 seconds
        sleep(60);
    }

    // Close file and I2C
    fclose(file);
    pigpio_i2c_close(i2c_handle);

    // Clean up
    pigpio_exit(gpio);

    return 0;

int main() {
    int i;
    int i2c_handle;
    FILE *file;
    float temperature;
    struct pigpio *gpio;
    struct pigpio_config config;

    // Initialize pigpio
    gpio = pigpio_init();
    if (gpio == NULL) {
        printf("Failed to initialize pigpio\n");
        return 1;
    }

    // Set up I2C configuration
    config.gpio_i2c_sda = 5;
    config.gpio_i2c_scl = 6;
    config.gpio_i2c_sda_pull = PI_GPIO_PULL_UP;
    config.gpio_i2c_scl_pull = PI_GPIO_PULL_UP;
    config.gpio_i2c_sda_edge = PI_GPIO_EDGE_RISING;
    config.gpio_i2c_scl_edge = PI_GPIO_EDGE_RISING;
    config.gpio_i2c_speed = PI_I2C_SPEED_100KHZ;

    // Initialize I2C
    i2c_handle = pigpio_i2c_open(&config);
    if (i2c_handle == -1) {
        printf("Failed to open I2C\n");
        pigpio_exit(gpio);
        return 1;
    }

    // Check device ID
    uint8_t device_id[3];
    if (pigpio_i2c_read(i2c_handle, I2C_ADDRESS, I2C_REG_DEVICE_ID, device_id, 3) != 3) {
        printf("Failed to read device ID\n");
        pigpio_i2c_close(i2c_handle);
        pigpio_exit(gpio);
        return 1;
    }
    if (memcmp(device_id, "0117", 3) != 0) {
        printf("Device ID mismatch\n");
        pigpio_i2c_close(i2c_handle);
        pigpio_exit(gpio);
        return 1;
    }

    // Open file for writing
    file = fopen("greenhouse_temps.dat", "wb");
    if (file == NULL) {
        printf("Failed to open file\n");
        pigpio_i2c_close(i2c_handle);
        pigpio_exit(gpio);
        return 1;
    }

    // Main loop
    while (1) {
        // Read temperature
        temperature = 0.0;
        if (pigpio_i2c_read(i2c_handle, I2C_ADDRESS, I2C_REG_TEMPERATURE, &temperature, 2) != 2) {
            printf("Failed to read temperature\n");
            break;
        }

        // Convert temperature to float
        temperature = (temperature * 0.0078125);

        // Write temperature to file
        fwrite(&temperature, sizeof(float), 1, file);

        // Sleep for 60 seconds
        sleep(60);
    }

    // Close file and I2C
    fclose(file);
    pigpio_i2c_close(i2c_handle);

    // Clean up
    pigpio_exit(gpio);

    return 0;
}

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (do NOT use wiringPi) to read differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP810-500Pa sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x25, simulating a basic HVAC airflow monitoring system. prompt: Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to control a solid-state relay on GPIO17, modulating a resistive heater to maintain a target temperature read from a MAX31855 thermocouple amplifier over the hardware SPI peripheral (SPI0, CE0: GPIO8 CS, GPIO9 MISO, GPIO10 MOSI, GPIO11 SCLK) at 2 MHz. Log temperature and PWM duty cycle to heater_log.csv with ISO-8601 timestamps. Implement a PI controller with anti-windup and a safe maximum duty cycle of 80% to prevent overheating. On SPI read failure or a MAX31855 fault (open circuit, short to GND, or short to VCC), immediately set the heater duty cycle to 0%, log the error, and continue running. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown — turn off the heater, close SPI, close the log file, terminate pigpio. The target temperature defaults to 25.0°C. Do not include any network or socket code.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to create a mood light that adjusts a common-anode RGB LED based on CPU temperature read from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp every 0.5 seconds. Red, Green, and Blue cathodes connect to GPIO 17, 18, and 27 (BCM), with the common anode on 3.3 V and current-limiting resistors on each cathode line. Use hardware PWM via gpioPWM (range 0-255) on each pin; since the LED is common-anode, a channel is fully off at duty 255 and fully on at duty 0, so invert the desired brightness accordingly. Apply temperature thresholds from the millidegree sysfs value: below 40000 m°C, solid Blue (R=0,G=0,B=255); 40000-59999 m°C, solid Green (R=0,G=255,B=0); 60000 m°C and above, solid Red (R=255,G=0,B=0). Print the current temperature (m°C) and RGB values to stdout each cycle. Check the return value of gpioInitialise(); on failure, print an error to stderr and exit with non-zero status. When reading the temperature file, handle both fopen failure and short or failed reads (check ferror); on any read error, print a diagnostic to stderr and skip the update cycle rather than using a bogus value, and close the file handle on every code path. Install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM, using a volatile sig_atomic_t flag and performing cleanup in main's exit path rather than inside the handler, so that Ctrl+C cleanly turns off all three channels (PWM duty 255 for common-anode off) and calls gpioTerminate() before exiting. Run an infinite loop until interrupted.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ to read humidity and temperature from a DHT22 sensor connected to GPIO4 (BCM numbering, physical pin 7), using the pigpio library for bit-banging the 1-wire protocol and libcurl for HTTP POST requests. Send a start signal by pulling the data line low for at least 1 ms, then read the 40-bit response. Parse the data, validate the 8-bit checksum, and POST the readings as a JSON payload to http://yourserver.com/api/humidity. Handle sensor-absent, checksum, and network errors gracefully with up to 3 retries. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library that toggles data logging from a BMP180 pressure sensor (I2C address 0x77 on bus 1) to pressure_log.txt via a push-button interrupt on GPIO4, containing timestamped pressure readings in hPa. Use a falling-edge ISR on GPIO4 with an internal pull-up to toggle logging on and off, debouncing in the ISR using pigpio tick comparison (at least 200000 us). Read the BMP180 calibration coefficients from registers 0xAA-0xBE at startup and validate them, failing cleanly if the sensor is absent or returns invalid data.
