prompt: Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that actively manages the official Raspberry Pi 5 Active Cooler through the sysfs thermal framework, using no third-party GPIO libraries. Read the CPU temperature (millidegrees Celsius) from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp every 5 seconds and write the fan state to /sys/class/thermal/cooling_device0/cur_state using a tiered speed map: below 45°C, state 0 (off); below 55°C, state 1; below 65°C, state 2; 65°C and above, state 3 (max). Validate the cooling device's max_state before writing, to ensure the requested state is within bounds. Check all file opens, reads, writes, and parses, and handle transient read failures by retrying on the next cycle. Log every fan speed change with a timestamp to /var/log/fan_control.log, but do not log when the speed has not changed. Implement graceful shutdown via SIGINT and SIGTERM: stop the fan (state 0), log the shutdown, and exit cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to implement a PID controller that maintains a target temperature by PWM-controlling a resistive heater on GPIO18 (hardware PWM, 1 kHz carrier, 0-100% duty). Read temperature from a MAX31855 thermocouple amplifier over SPI0 (CLK=GPIO11, CS=GPIO8/CE0, DO=GPIO9) at 500 kHz, reading 4 bytes per sample. Log the temperature, PWM duty cycle, and PID output to heater_log.txt every second. Handle SPI communication errors and thermocouple faults — open circuit, short to GND, short to VCC — by parsing the MAX31855 fault bits, logging errors to the same file, disabling the heater, and resetting the PID state. Include a failsafe that disables the heater if the reading exceeds 100°C or falls below 0°C. Ensure clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM: heater off, SPI closed, pigpio terminated. Use Kp=1.0, Ki=0.1, Kd=0.01, and target=50°C as defaults.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to modulate a 25 kHz PWM signal on GPIO18 (physical pin 12) to control a Noctua NF-A4x10 5V PWM fan, dynamically adjusting fan speed based on CPU temperature read from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp (in millidegrees Celsius). Use a linear mapping: 0% duty at 40°C and below, 100% duty at 70°C and above, with linear interpolation in between. Log the timestamp, temperature (°C), and PWM duty cycle (as a 0-100 percentage) to a comma-separated file cooling_log.csv with a CSV header, polling the temperature every 5 seconds. Check pigpio initialization, verify the PWM frequency and duty cycle calls, handle file I/O errors, and gracefully shut down on SIGINT/SIGTERM by turning off the fan and releasing resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to interface with two Sensirion SLF3S-1300F liquid flow sensors on I2C bus 1. Both sensors share the default I2C address 0x08, so assume they are connected through a Sensirion SF06 multiplexer breakout (or similar I2C hub) that maps them to addresses 0x08 and 0x09. Continuously poll both sensors every 1 second using the SLF3S-1300F continuous measurement command 0x3608, reading 3 bytes per sensor (2 data bytes plus 1 CRC byte) and validating the CRC-8 checksum, skipping the logging if the CRC fails. Convert readings using raw_value * 0.01 to get flow rate in ml/min. Log the flow rates to a comma-separated file named flow_log.txt (format YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,flow1,flow2). Handle I2C errors robustly with up to 3 retries per sensor. Implement clean shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM, closing all I2C handles and terminating pigpio.

Develop a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to monitor a magnetic rotary encoder built from two TMAG5110A1 Hall-Effect Latch sensors: Sensor A (Channel A) on GPIO17 and Sensor B (Channel B) on GPIO18. Since the TMAG5110A1 has an open-drain output, configure internal pull-up resistors on both pins. Implement a standard 2-bit quadrature state machine to track rotation increments over 360 pulses per revolution, logging every state change with a timestamp and the normalized angular position (0.00 to 360.00 degrees) to encoder_log.txt. Ensure robust error handling for GPIO initialization and file I/O, and implement clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM using pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using libgpiod for GPIO and the Linux I2C character-device interface (linux/i2c-dev.h) to interface with an Analog Devices ADPD144RI red and infrared photometric sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default 7-bit address 0x39. Read the 16-bit red and IR channel data from the FIFO data register (0x60), handling I2C read/write errors and sensor-absent conditions. Trigger an LED on GPIO 17 (active-high) if the IR reading exceeds a threshold of 2000. Sample every 100 ms and log timestamped readings to adpd144ri_log.txt in CSV format (timestamp,red,ir). Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, cleanly releasing all resources — the I2C file descriptor, GPIO lines, and log file — on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to read RPM from a Melexis MLX90254 magnetic speed sensor connected to GPIO 18 (physical pin 12, configured as input with a pull-down), which outputs 1 pulse per revolution. Calculate RPM over a 1-second interval by counting rising edges only, and log RPM values with timestamps to rpm_log.txt in append mode, flushed immediately. Use a pthread mutex to protect the pulse counter between the ISR and the main thread. Check pigpio initialization, ISR registration, and log file opening. Use a signal handler for SIGINT/SIGTERM for graceful shutdown that terminates pigpio, closes the log file, and destroys the mutex. If the sensor is absent (0 pulses), log 0.00 RPM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using libgpiod and the standard Linux I2C interface (/dev/i2c-1) to interface with an Analog Devices ADPD144RI red and infrared photometric sensor at I2C address 0x39. Read the PART_ID register (0x00) to verify the sensor is present, then read the red and IR channel data from the FIFO data registers, handling I2C errors and sensor-absent paths robustly. Trigger an LED on GPIO 17 if the IR reading exceeds a threshold of 2000. Sample every 100 ms and log timestamped readings to adpd144ri_log.txt in CSV format. Clean up all resources — the I2C bus, GPIO lines, and log file — on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT/SIGTERM. Do not use the deprecated bcm2835 or wiringPi libraries.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 using the libgpiod API (not sysfs or wiringPi) to sample the analog audio output of an Adafruit MAX9814 Electret Microphone Amplifier. Connect the MAX9814 OUT pin to GPIO 17 (configured as input) and the GAIN pin to GPIO 18 (configured as output), setting GPIO 18 LOW to select 60dB gain. Since the MAX9814 provides an analog signal, rapidly poll the digital input pin, at a 10 ms interval, to detect rising edges (logic HIGH) as peak sound events. Log each detected peak to audio_log.txt with a timestamp formatted as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS LEVEL', where LEVEL is 1 for a rising edge. Handle all libgpiod initialization and I/O errors robustly, checking the return value of every API call, and ensure clean release of all libgpiod resources on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling. Print a startup message and run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to monitor flow rate from a Sensirion SLF3S-4000B Liquid Flow Sensor connected on I2C bus 1 at the default 7-bit address 0x36, for a microfluidic drug delivery system. Initialize the sensor by sending the 2-byte command 0x3608 to start continuous measurement. Every 1000 ms, read 3 bytes from the sensor: a 16-bit raw flow value (MSB first) followed by a CRC-8 byte, and validate it using the Sensirion CRC-8 algorithm (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF); if the CRC check fails, log an error and skip that reading. Convert the raw 16-bit signed value to a flow rate in uL/min by dividing by 1000.0. Log each valid reading to a CSV file named 'flow_log.csv' in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,flow_rate_uL_min', opening the file once at startup in append mode, keeping it open, and flushing after each write rather than reopening repeatedly. Check every pigpio initialization, I2C open, write, and read call; on an I2C read or write failure, log the error to stderr and attempt to recover on the next loop iteration. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) gracefully by closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and terminating pigpio.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to poll a KY-033 Obstacle Avoidance Sensor Module connected to GPIO 4 (BCM numbering, physical pin 7), which outputs LOW (0) when an obstacle is detected within its threshold and HIGH (1) otherwise. Initialize pigpio and verify success, printing an error to stderr and returning non-zero on failure. Configure GPIO 4 as input with the internal pull-up resistor enabled and poll it every 50 ms. On each detection (reading == 0), record a timestamp and the reading into a circular buffer of 100 entries that overwrites the oldest entry when full, and print an alert to stdout. On SIGINT (Ctrl+C), print the entire buffer contents in chronological order with human-readable timestamps, release all pigpio resources, and exit cleanly. Do not use any deprecated APIs.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 (64-bit Bookworm) that interfaces with an Omron D7S vibration sensor over I2C (up to 400 kHz, default 7-bit address 0x55) using the Linux I2C character-device API (open()/ioctl(I2C_SLAVE)/read()/write() on /dev/i2c-1, GPIO 2/3 for SDA/SCL) to detect subtle vibrations indicating pre-failure in a small cooling fan. Initialize the sensor by writing 0x10 to register 0x1D (MODE_CONTROL) to switch it from standby to active mode, then wait until the operating-status register (0x1B) bit 0 reads 1; if the sensor does not become active within 1 second, print an error and exit. Every 500 ms, read the 16-bit signed acceleration registers X (0x2A/0x2B), Y (0x2C/0x2D), and Z (0x2E/0x2F), little-endian with LSB first, and convert the raw values to g using the scaling factor 0.0009765625 g/LSB. Log each sample as a CSV row with an ISO-8601 timestamp to 'fan_health.csv' in append mode, writing a header row if the file is newly created. Check every I2C syscall return value; on a read/write/ioctl failure, print a diagnostic to stderr and retry on the next iteration rather than crashing. Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM cleanly by closing the I2C file descriptor and the CSV file, then exit. The program should run until interrupted by the user.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to interface with two Keywish KY-032 Infrared Obstacle Avoidance sensors (active-LOW outputs, logic 0 = obstacle detected) connected to GPIO 23 (Sensor 1 OUT) and GPIO 24 (Sensor 2 OUT), triggering an LED on GPIO 25 (through a 220-330 ohm resistor to GND) when an obstacle is detected within approximately 10 cm of either sensor. Poll both sensors every 100 ms. Turn the LED ON immediately when either sensor reads LOW, and turn it OFF when both read HIGH. Verify pigpio initialization, validate every gpioSetMode/gpioRead/gpioWrite return code, and ensure clean resource release (gpioTerminate) on all exit paths, including SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to monitor a conveyor belt with two E18-D80NK IR obstacle sensors connected to GPIO 17 and GPIO 18, which output LOW (0) when an object is detected and HIGH (1) when clear. A stall is confirmed when both sensors read LOW continuously for at least 2 seconds; on a confirmed stall, log a timestamped entry to 'stall_log.txt', avoiding duplicate log entries for the same stall event. Check pigpio initialization, validate every sensor read, handle file I/O errors, and ensure clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to interface with a Texas Instruments TMAG5170-Q1 I2C 3D Hall-Effect sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x0E (A0=A1=0). Configure the sensor for continuous-conversion mode with all three axes enabled and a 50 mT range. Verify the device ID register (0x00, expected value 0x8D) at startup, and write a CSV header row to 'magnetic_log.csv' if the file is newly created. Every 100 ms, read the X, Y, and Z magnetic field readings, convert the raw 16-bit two's-complement values to mT using the appropriate LSB scale factor for the 50 mT range, and log them with ISO-8601 timestamps to 'magnetic_log.csv'. Check every I2C read/write return code, and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths by logging errors to stderr and continuing. Register a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler for clean resource release (close the I2C handle, close the file, call gpioTerminate). Run an infinite loop until interrupted by Ctrl+C.

Write a robust C daemon for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to monitor a SEN0193 Water Level Sensor (digital output) connected to GPIO 23, using a pull-down resistor on the input to avoid floating states when the sensor is dry. Poll the sensor every 2 seconds. When water is detected (logic HIGH), print an alert message to stdout and append a timestamped entry in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS ALERT: Water detected' to 'flood_log.txt'. Check pigpio initialization, handle GPIO read failures with an automatic re-initialization attempt after 60 seconds (logging error entries to the same log file), and ensure clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B (Bookworm or later) using the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to read RPM from a Melexis MLX90217 Hall-effect sensor via GPIO interrupts. The sensor output is connected to physical pin 7 (Broadcom GPIO 4), configured as input with the internal pull-up resistor enabled. Count rising-edge pulses in a 1-second window using an atomic add for the pulse counter, and compute RPM as pulses_per_second * 60, assuming one pulse per revolution. Every 1-second sample, log 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS <rpm>' to 'rpm_log.txt' (flushing the file after each write) and print it to stdout, logging RPM 0 rather than aborting when the sensor is absent or not rotating. Check every pigpio call and file-open call for errors and exit with a diagnostic message on failure. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers so Ctrl+C stops cleanly: disable the timer and alert callback, close the log file, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to detect direction of rotation from two Melexis MLX90217 unipolar Hall-effect sensors connected to GPIO 17 (Sensor A) and GPIO 27 (Sensor B) via hardware pull-up resistors, physically offset by 90 degrees to produce a quadrature signal. Use pigpio alerts (gpioSetAlertFunc) for edge-triggered interrupts instead of polling, and implement a quadrature state machine that tracks the previous state to determine direction, protecting the shared state between the ISR and main loop with a mutex. Log each detected rotation event (CW or CCW) with a millisecond-precision timestamp (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.mmm) to 'rotation_log.txt'. Check all error paths: gpioInitialise(), gpioSetAlertFunc(), gpioSetPullUpDown(), and file open. Use a signal handler (SIGINT/SIGTERM) for graceful shutdown, ensuring the log file is flushed/closed and pigpio is terminated. The main loop should wait on a condition variable or sleep, not busy-spin. Never use wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the libgpiod library's line request API to interface with a SainSmart TTP223B digital capacitive touch sensor whose OUT pin is connected to GPIO 23 (physical pin 16), and an LED on GPIO 18 (physical pin 12) with a current-limiting resistor. Poll the touch sensor every 50 ms (to avoid busy-waiting) and illuminate the LED only while the sensor is actively touched. Check all libgpiod calls, including chip opening, line requests, reads, and writes, handling the case where the GPIO chip is unavailable. Log all touch events, errors, and startup/shutdown messages to the system syslog using openlog/syslog. Implement graceful shutdown via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handlers to ensure the LED is turned off and resources are released before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the libgpiod library's line event interface to read touch input from a SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensor connected to GPIO 17 (physical pin 11), which outputs HIGH (3.3 V) when touched and LOW when idle. On each rising-edge touch detection (with approximately 50 ms software debounce), toggle an LED connected to GPIO 18 (physical pin 12). Initialize the LED line as output and drive it LOW at startup. Check every libgpiod call (chip open, line request, event wait, read, write) and print meaningful messages to stderr on failure. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully: release all libgpiod resources (lines and chip) and exit cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to interface with two SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensors (active-high) on GPIO 4 and GPIO 17, each controlling a distinct LED on GPIO 27 and GPIO 22 respectively, lit while the corresponding sensor is touched. Use a 50 ms polling loop for debounce. Log every touch and release event (sensor pin, Unix timestamp, and new state) into a 100-entry circular buffer in RAM with an overflow counter tracking how many events were overwritten once the buffer wraps. Check the return value of gpioInitialise and every gpioSetMode/gpioWrite/gpioRead call, printing a diagnostic to stderr on any failure. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, turning off both LEDs and calling gpioTerminate before exiting. On shutdown, print the full log buffer contents and the overflow count to stdout.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to monitor a Raindrop Sensor Module (digital output, active-low: reads LOW (0) when rain is detected, HIGH (1) when dry) connected to GPIO 17, with the internal pull-up resistor enabled so the input is defined when the sensor is disconnected. Poll the sensor every 500 ms and log only state transitions, writing timestamped 'Rain Detected' or 'No Rain' messages to /var/log/rain_events.log. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, closing the log file and releasing pigpio resources on all exit paths. Check the return value of every pigpio call and of fopen.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to monitor a rotating shaft's RPM using two DRV5032FJDBZR Hall-Effect sensors (push-pull outputs, 3.3 V) connected to GPIO 17 and GPIO 18. Implement a debounce mechanism (approximately 5 ms) to avoid false readings, and calculate and print the RPM to the console assuming 2 pulses per revolution. Log timestamps and sensor state changes to a CSV file named 'shaft_log.txt' in the format 'timestamp,sensor1_state,sensor2_state'. Handle potential GPIO initialization and file I/O errors gracefully, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT (Ctrl+C). Include all required standard headers (e.g., errno.h, string.h) so the code compiles cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to read heart rate and SpO2 data from a Silicon Labs Si1182 I2C-based optical sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x28. Initialize pigpio, open the I2C bus, and verify the sensor is present by reading the PART_ID register at 0x00. Configure the sensor for continuous measurement by writing to the CONFIG register at 0x30. Once per second, read heart rate data from register 0x02 and SpO2 data from register 0x04, and log each reading with a timestamp in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, Heart Rate: X BPM, SpO2: Y%%' to 'biometric_log.txt' in append mode, flushing after each write. Check every I2C read/write return value and handle failures; on communication errors, print a message to stderr and continue the loop. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle and log file and terminating pigpio before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to monitor structural integrity of a miniature bridge model using two digital tilt sensors, which output HIGH when tilted beyond their threshold, connected to GPIO 17 (sensor 1) and GPIO 18 (sensor 2), both configured as inputs with internal pull-down resistors enabled. Connect an active-high alarm (buzzer/LED) to GPIO 27, initialized LOW. Poll at a 100 ms interval using gpioDelay. If either sensor reads HIGH continuously for more than 2 seconds, activate the alarm (GPIO 27 HIGH); when both sensors return to LOW, deactivate the alarm. Log all tilt-start, threshold-exceeded, and tilt-end events with ISO-8601 timestamps (YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS) to 'bridge_integrity.log'. Check pigpio initialization, log file opening, and gpioRead return values. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for clean shutdown (deactivate the alarm, close the log file, call gpioTerminate), ensuring the alarm is deactivated on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to interface with an Omron D7S-A0011 seismic sensor over I2C bus 1 (default 7-bit address 0x1D, SDA=GPIO2, SCL=GPIO3). Initialize the sensor by verifying its presence and clearing the power-down bit in CTRL1 (register 0x1F). Every 100 ms, poll the 3-axis acceleration registers (0x28-0x2D, little-endian, 6-byte block read) and compute the Euclidean vibration magnitude; if it exceeds a threshold of 500, turn on an LED on GPIO 17 for 1 second, then turn it off. Log every threshold-exceeding event with an ISO-8601 timestamp and the peak vibration value to 'seismic_events.log'. Handle I2C communication errors and sensor-absent conditions gracefully with up to 3 retries per read. Ensure all resources (I2C handle, pigpio library, log file) are released cleanly on Ctrl+C/SIGINT. Build with: gcc -O2 -Wall -o seismic seismic.c -lpigpio -lm -lrt.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 using the libgpiod library to read obstacle detection data from four Keywish KY-032 Infrared Obstacle Avoidance Sensors whose OUT pins are connected to GPIO 4, 17, 27, and 22 (active-low: 0 = object detected). If any sensor detects an object, turn ON an LED connected to GPIO 18; otherwise turn it OFF. Poll the lines every 50 ms. Robustly handle GPIO initialization errors (e.g., chip open, line request failures) and cleanly release all resources on SIGINT/SIGTERM. Do not use blocking delays that would prevent prompt signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using libgpiod (v1.6+) to monitor 5 Keyes KY-026 flame sensors on BCM GPIO 2, 3, 4, 17, and 27 (physical pins 3, 5, 7, 11, 13), wiring each sensor's digital output (LOW when a flame is detected, HIGH otherwise) to its GPIO and VCC/GND to 3.3V and GND. Poll all five lines once per second. On a rising-edge transition from no-flame to flame, confirmed by a 50 ms debounce re-read, append an event line to /var/log/flame_events.log formatted as '<ISO 8601 UTC timestamp> - Sensor ID: <id> (GPIO <pin>) - Flame Detected'. Use syslog (facility LOG_USER, ident 'flame_monitor') for startup, read-error, and shutdown messages. Check every libgpiod call (chip open, line get, line request, line read) and every file I/O call (fopen, flock, fprintf, fflush); log and continue on per-sensor read failures rather than aborting, aborting only if chip open or line acquisition/request fails. Install SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers that set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, release all requested lines, close the chip, and call closelog() on both normal and error paths. Track individual line pointers in an array rather than using gpiod_line_bulk_* APIs. Compile with: gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o flame_monitor flame_monitor.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the libgpiod v1.x API to read the 8 individual touch states from a TTP226 8-channel capacitive touch sensor whose outputs OUT0-OUT7 are connected to BCM GPIO pins 5, 6, 13, 19, 26, 12, 16, and 20 respectively. Poll all eight pins every 50 milliseconds, logging only state changes (touch detected / released) to the console with ISO-8601 timestamps and the sensor index plus BCM pin number. Implement robust error handling for GPIO chip initialization, line resolution, bulk line requests, and read failures, printing a descriptive error (including errno) and exiting with a non-zero status on unrecoverable failures. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown on SIGINT (Ctrl+C). The code must compile cleanly with gcc -Wall -Wextra -lgpiod and must not rely on libgpiod v2-only APIs such as struct gpiod_line_bulk.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to implement an adaptive grow light system with a VEML7700 lux sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x10. Configure the sensor with ALS gain 1/8 (0x00) and ALS integration time 100 ms (0x00) by writing a 16-bit value to config register 0x00 (little-endian: low byte first, high byte second). Read ambient light from ALS register 0x04 (16-bit little-endian) once per second and convert it to lux using lux = raw * 0.0576. Control an LED on GPIO 18 via hardware PWM at 1000 Hz with range 0-100, using adaptive brightness logic: lux < 100 -> 100%, lux < 500 -> 75%, lux < 1000 -> 50%, lux >= 1000 -> 25%. Log each sample to 'grow_log.txt' with an ISO timestamp, lux value, brightness, and error code, flushing after each write. Check pigpio initialization, I2C open, sensor config write, ALS read, and PWM operations; log and handle sensor-absent/bus-error paths. On SIGINT/SIGTERM, turn off the LED, close I2C, close the log file, and terminate pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library for a simulated security keypad that interfaces with an 8-channel TTP226 capacitive touch sensor module whose 8 digital output channels are connected to GPIO 2-9 (BCM numbering), and an LED on GPIO 17 that lights whenever any touch is detected. Initialize pigpio and verify success, exiting with an error message on failure; configure GPIO 2-9 as inputs with pull-down resistors and GPIO 17 as an output. Poll the inputs every 50 ms and debounce each channel so a single touch is logged only once per press. Log each new touch event to 'touch_log.txt' in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS - Channel X Touched', where X (1-8) corresponds to GPIO 2-9. Turn the LED on when any channel transitions from untouched to touched, and off when all channels are released. Check all file I/O operations for errors and print diagnostics to stderr. Implement a clean signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that turns off the LED, releases pigpio resources, and exits gracefully.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to read ambient light data from a Texas Instruments OPT3001 sensor for a smart greenhouse environment monitoring system. Use I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1, pigpio bus 1), OPT3001 address 0x44, configuration register 0x01, and result register 0x00. Configure the sensor for continuous conversion mode with automatic full-scale range and a 100 ms conversion time using configuration word 0xC810; pigpio's i2cReadWordData/i2cWriteWordData use little-endian word order while the OPT3001 expects/reports big-endian (MSB first), so byte-swap the 16-bit values before writing and after reading. After writing the configuration, wait at least 100 ms for the first conversion before reading the result register. Once per second, read the 16-bit result register, where bits 15-12 are the exponent and bits 11-0 are the mantissa, and compute lux = mantissa * 0.01 * (2^exponent). Log each reading to 'light_data.txt' as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, <lux_value>' with two decimal places, and also print the lux value to stdout for live monitoring. Check the return value of every pigpio and file I/O call; if i2cOpen or i2cReadWordData fails, print a descriptive error to stderr and skip that iteration, or exit gracefully on init failure. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library to poll three KY-033 obstacle-avoidance sensors (IR reflective, digital output) wired to GPIO17 (left), GPIO27 (middle), and GPIO22 (right). Poll all three lines every 50 ms and append each reading (0 or 1 per sensor) with an ISO-8601 timestamp to a CSV file named 'path_log.csv' with columns timestamp,left,middle,right. Verify that the gpiochip opens successfully, that each line can be requested as input, and that file I/O succeeds. Handle SIGINT cleanly by releasing all GPIO lines, closing the chip, flushing, and closing the log file before exiting. Include the necessary system headers, such as errno.h and stdbool.h, so the code compiles without warnings under gcc -Wall -Wextra.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library (not pigpio or wiringPi) to monitor a Keyes KY-026 flame sensor (digital output, active-low: 0 = flame detected, 1 = no flame) connected to GPIO4 (BCM). Use edge-based event polling on the falling edge for efficient detection. When a flame is detected, print an alert with a timestamp to stdout and log the event, with its timestamp, to 'flame_events.txt'. Verify that the libgpiod chip and line requests succeed, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library (not sysfs, not wiringPi) to interface with a TTP223 capacitive touch sensor on GPIO23 (BCM 23, input, active-high) and toggle an LED on GPIO24 (BCM 24, output). Use libgpiod line events on the rising edge (touch detected) with a 1-second poll timeout, toggling the LED on each event; debounce is not required since the TTP223 has built-in hardware debouncing. Log every touch event with an ISO-8601 timestamp and the new LED state to 'touch_log.txt'. Open GPIO chip /dev/gpiochip4; if it cannot be opened or its lines cannot be requested, exit with an error after cleaning up any partially initialized resources. Check every libgpiod call and file operation for errors and report failures to stderr; if the log file cannot be opened, exit with an error. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown by releasing all libgpiod resources and closing the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod character-device API (gpiod_chip_open_by_name, gpiod_chip_get_line, gpiod_line_request_input, gpiod_line_request_output, gpiod_line_get_value, gpiod_line_set_value on device 'gpiochip0'; not wiringPi or sysfs) to implement a flame-detection safety system with a Keyes KY-026 flame sensor and an active buzzer. The KY-026 digital-output pin is connected to GPIO17 (physical pin 11) and is active-low: it reads LOW when a flame is detected and HIGH otherwise. An active buzzer is connected to GPIO18 (physical pin 12) and sounds when its control line is driven HIGH. Poll the flame sensor every 500 ms. On a HIGH-to-LOW transition (software edge detection, not continuously while the line stays LOW), log the event with a timestamp to 'alert_log.txt' and activate the buzzer for 2 seconds, then continue. Log a 'System started' entry at startup and a 'System stopped' entry on clean shutdown. Break the 2-second buzzer activation and the 500 ms poll interval into 100 ms slices so the program can respond promptly to shutdown signals. Check every libgpiod call, file operation, and syscall for failure, printing a diagnostic via strerror(errno) to stderr and exiting non-zero if initialization fails. Include the headers errno.h, string.h, time.h, signal.h, unistd.h, stdio.h, stdlib.h, and gpiod.h. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown: turn the buzzer off, release the lines, close the chip, close the log file, and exit cleanly with code 0. Build with: gcc -Wall -Wextra -O2 -o flame_alert flame_alert.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to read a SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensor on GPIO4 (physical pin 7) and toggle an LED on GPIO17 (physical pin 11). The TTP223B outputs HIGH (3.3 V) when touched and LOW when released. Configure GPIO4 as input and GPIO17 as output, checking all return values and reporting errors to stderr. Poll GPIO4 every 10 ms; on a rising edge (LOW-to-HIGH transition, not just level), toggle the LED and append a UTC ISO-8601 timestamped line to 'touch_log.txt'. Implement a 200 ms software debounce so a single touch does not register multiple events. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown by turning off the LED, closing the log file, and calling gpioTerminate(). If the log file cannot be opened, print an error and exit non-zero; if a write to it fails, print a warning to stderr but continue running.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to interface with three Texas Instruments TMAG5110A1 Hall-effect latch magnetic sensors on GPIO4, GPIO17, and GPIO27 (BCM numbering). Each sensor's open-drain OUT pin drives a GPIO input with an internal pull-up enabled: it pulls low when a south pole is present and releases high otherwise, so a logic low means magnet-present and a logic high means magnet-removed. Initialize pigpio and verify every GPIO mode and pull call returns 0. Poll all three sensors every 100 ms using gpioDelay, and on the first read record the initial state without falsely logging a transition. Log each state change, with an ISO-8601 timestamp and sensor identifier, to 'magnet_log.txt'. Handle sensor read errors gracefully by logging to stderr and continuing. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers for clean shutdown that close the log file and call gpioTerminate(). Include comments explaining the latch behavior.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to read heart-rate data from a Silicon Labs Si1182-A-GM optical heart-rate sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x4A. Initialize pigpio and open the I2C bus, checking every return code. Verify the sensor's PART_ID register (0x00) reads 0x02 and HW_REV register (0x01) reads 0x01, aborting with a clear error if the sensor is absent or wrong. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod C library (v1.x API, not wiringPi) to read a Keywish 3-Way Tracking Sensor (IR reflectance, digital GPIO) connected to Broadcom GPIO pins 2 (left), 3 (middle), and 4 (right). Poll all three lines every 100 ms and log the sensor values to stdout in the format 'L:<0|1> M:<0|1> R:<0|1>'. Use individual gpiod_line_request_input calls (not the bulk API) to maximize portability across libgpiod versions. Check every libgpiod call, including chip open, line get, line request, and line read, and handle the case where the gpiochip device is absent or permission-denied. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, using signal handling for SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to terminate gracefully.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library (v1.x API: gpiod_line, gpiod_chip, gpiod_line_get_value; not wiringPi) to read a TTP226 8-channel capacitive touch sensor, whose 8 independent active-high output lines TP1-TP8 connect to BCM GPIO 5, 6, 13, 19, 26, 12, 16, and 20 respectively. Open gpiochip0 and request all 8 lines as inputs. Poll every 200 ms and log each channel's state (0 or 1) to the console in a single timestamped line using a monotonic clock, for example '[12.345s] CH1=0 CH2=1 CH3=0 CH4=0 CH5=0 CH6=0 CH7=0 CH8=0'. Handle errors at every step, including chip-open failure, line-request failure, and individual line-read failure, printing to stderr and exiting with non-zero status. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler for graceful shutdown that releases all libgpiod resources (lines, chip) cleanly before exiting. Provide compile instructions in a comment.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to create a standalone 'mood lamp' with a common-anode RGB LED connected to GPIO17 (Red), GPIO18 (Green), and GPIO27 (Blue). Smoothly fade between randomly chosen hues every 5 seconds using hardware PWM at 1000 Hz with an 8-bit (0-255) range, applying a 50-step linear interpolation over each 5-second fade. Because the LED is common-anode, invert every PWM duty-cycle value as 255 minus the value, and clamp all color channel values to [0, 255]. Convert each random hue to RGB using the standard HSV-to-RGB algorithm with full saturation and value; select hues internally via rand() seeded from /dev/urandom, with no networking or external message bus required. Check pigpio initialization and every gpioPWM/gpioSetMode return value, logging errors via syslog. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown by turning off the LED, releasing pigpio resources, and closing syslog.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the libgpiod library for GPIO control and the Linux i2c-dev ioctl interface (not wiringPi) to interface with a TCS34725 color sensor over I2C bus /dev/i2c-1 (BCM pins 2/3) at its fixed address 0x29. Initialize the sensor by powering it on (PON) and enabling RGBC (AEN), set the integration time to approximately 154 ms (ATIME=0x00) and gain to 1x (CONTROL=0x00), and verify the sensor ID register (0x12) returns 0x44 before proceeding. Read all four 16-bit channel registers as little-endian pairs: clear (0x14), red (0x16), green (0x18), and blue (0x1A). Apply per-channel gain and offset calibration and display the calibrated RGB and clear (C) values on the console. Drive an LED on GPIO17 HIGH when the calibrated red value exceeds a threshold of 200, and LOW otherwise. Check every open, ioctl, read, and write return value; attempt sensor re-initialization on a read failure. Ensure clean resource release, closing the I2C file descriptor, releasing the GPIO line, and powering down the sensor, on all exit paths including SIGINT and SIGTERM. Poll the sensor every 200 ms.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to control the brightness of a 10-LED WS2812B strip connected to GPIO18 (PCM_CLK/GPIO18), generating the precise WS2812B timing waveform via pigpio's hardware PWM/wave functionality. Read ambient light levels from a BH1750 I2C digital light sensor at address 0x23 using continuous high-resolution mode (command 0x10): wait approximately 180 ms after issuing the command, then read 2 bytes and compute lux = (MSB<<8 | LSB) / 1.2. Implement a smooth, non-linear (logarithmic) brightness mapping from the light-sensor readings (0-1000 lux) to LED strip brightness. Gracefully handle I2C errors and sensor-absent conditions with retries, and cleanly release all resources on SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads ambient light from a BH1750 I2C sensor at address 0x23 and adjusts the brightness of an APA102 LED strip via SPI proportionally to the measured lux. Use the Linux I2C (/dev/i2c-1) and SPI (/dev/spidev0.0) character devices directly; do not use the deprecated wiringPi library. Sample every 100 ms, reading the range status register (0x04d) to detect errors such as overrange or signal failure. Check all I2C read/write return values and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths by attempting re-initialization. Handle SIGINT for clean resource release.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses pigpio to sample data from two STMicroelectronics IMP23ABSU ultrasonic MEMS microphone sensors on I2C bus 1, simulating a bat echolocation analysis system. The two sensors have distinct I2C addresses: sensor 1 at 0x68 and sensor 2 at 0x69, each exposing a 16-bit data register at 0x01 and a control register at 0x00 that must be written with 0x80 to enable continuous measurement. Read 16-bit signed audio samples from both sensors, timestamp them using CLOCK_REALTIME, compute a basic Time Difference of Arrival (TDOA) by subtracting the two samples, and log the data as CSV to 'audio_log.dat' with columns sec, nsec, sensor1, sensor2, tdoa. Use a 10 ms sampling interval. Verify all pigpio initialization and I2C communication calls; handle sensor-absent or bus-failure paths gracefully by skipping the sample and retrying. Ensure clean resource release (I2C handles, log file, pigpio termination) on all exit paths via a SIGINT signal handler.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface over SPI with an Analog Devices ADIS16488A IMU on SPI channel 0 (CE0 on GPIO8) at 1 MHz, SPI mode 3 (CPOL=1, CPHA=1), using pigpio SPI flags 0b11000000000 (bit 9 = CPHA, bit 10 = CPOL, bit 8 = aux SPI off) and 16-bit words. The ADIS16488A read protocol sends a 16-bit word whose MSB is 0 followed by the 7-bit register address; the requested register's data is returned on the next 16-bit transfer, so implement a dummy read or stall of at least 40 microseconds between the request and the data-retrieval transfer. Continuously read gyroscope X, Y, Z from registers X_GYRO=0x04, Y_GYRO=0x06, Z_GYRO=0x08 and accelerometer X, Y, Z from X_ACCEL=0x0A, Y_ACCEL=0x0C, Z_ACCEL=0x0E every 100 ms, converting with sensitivities 0.005 deg/sec/LSB for gyroscope and 0.00025 g/LSB for accelerometer, and log each sample with a millisecond-precision timestamp to a CSV file named "imu_data.csv" whose header row is "timestamp,gyro_x,gyro_y,gyro_z,accel_x,accel_y,accel_z". Check the return values of gpioInitialise, spiOpen and fopen; if spiXfer returns less than 0, log the error to stderr and skip that sample rather than aborting. Use a non-blocking sampling delay that checks a running flag every few milliseconds so the program responds promptly to signals, and implement a cleanup() helper registered with atexit() that closes the SPI handle and CSV file and terminates pigpio on SIGINT, SIGTERM and every other exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads an Analog Devices ADIS16448 IMU over SPI bus 0, chip-select CS0 on GPIO8, SPI mode 3, at up to 1 MHz. Because libgpiod has no SPI API, perform the SPI transfers through the Linux spidev ioctl interface and use libgpiod only for the chip-select/GPIO line. Use the ADIS16448 single-register read protocol: send the 8-bit register address with bit 7 set (0x80) in the first 16-bit SPI cycle, then read the 16-bit data response in the second cycle. Read gyroscope X, Y, Z from XGYRO_OUT=0x04, YGYRO_OUT=0x06, ZGYRO_OUT=0x08 and accelerometer X, Y, Z from XACCL_OUT=0x0A, YACCL_OUT=0x0C, ZACCL_OUT=0x0E, applying scale factors of 0.02 dps/LSB for gyroscope and 0.00025 g/LSB for accelerometer, and log the values to the console every 100 ms. Include robust error handling for SPI initialization, ioctl transfers and data reads, and handle SIGINT/SIGTERM for clean resource release by closing the SPI device file and the libgpiod chip.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with an Analog Devices ADIS16448 IMU over SPI channel 0 (CE0/GPIO8) at 1 MHz, SPI Mode 0. The ADIS16448 requires a two-cycle SPI read: send the read command (register address with bit 15 set) in the first 16-bit transfer, wait at least 40 microseconds of stall time, then send a dummy 0x0000 in the second transfer to clock out the 16-bit data. Periodically read gyroscope x, y, z from X_GYRO_OUT=0x04, Y_GYRO_OUT=0x06, Z_GYRO_OUT=0x08 and accelerometer x, y, z from X_ACCL_OUT=0x0A, Y_ACCL_OUT=0x0C, Z_ACCL_OUT=0x0E, scaling with 0.05 deg/sec/LSB for gyroscope and 0.00025 g/LSB for accelerometer, and print the formatted values to the console every 100 ms. Include robust error handling for pigpio initialization, SPI open, and transfer failures, and handle Ctrl+C cleanly by closing the SPI handle and calling gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a TDK MPU-6886 6-axis IMU over I2C bus 1 at address 0x68 using the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface (open/ioctl/read/write), not wiringPi. Verify the sensor is present by reading the WHO_AM_I register (0x75) and checking it returns 0x86, then initialize the sensor by waking it (PWR_MGMT_1 = 0x00) and setting ACCEL_CONFIG (0x1C) and GYRO_CONFIG (0x1B) to 0x00 for the +-2g and +-250 dps ranges. Every 50 ms, read raw accelerometer data from registers 0x3B-0x40 and gyroscope data from registers 0x43-0x48, and print the raw 16-bit signed values to the console. Check every I2C syscall, retry transient read failures up to 3 times, and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths gracefully, ensuring clean resource release by closing the I2C file descriptor on all exit paths including SIGINT (Ctrl+C).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library for I2C and GPIO to interface with an Adafruit ADXL345 accelerometer on I2C bus 1 at address 0x53, configured for full-resolution mode at the +-2g range (scale factor 256 LSB/g), to detect sudden impacts. Verify the ADXL345 device ID by reading register 0x00 and checking it equals 0xE5. Poll the sensor every 10 ms; if the total acceleration magnitude exceeds 2.5g, turn on a red LED connected to GPIO17 for 500 ms and append a timestamped entry containing the magnitude and X/Y/Z components to "impact_log.txt". Check every I2C read/write call, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release of the I2C handle, LED, log file, and pigpio on all exit paths including SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library for all I2C operations to read accelerometer and gyroscope data from a TDK InvenSense ICM-20602 IMU on I2C bus 1 at address 0x68. Initialize the device by waking it from sleep (PWR_MGMT_1 = 0x00), setting the accelerometer to +-2g (ACCEL_CONFIG = 0x00) and the gyroscope to +-250 dps (GYRO_CONFIG = 0x00), and before the main loop verify the sensor is present by reading the WHO_AM_I register (0x75) and checking for the expected value 0x12. Use burst reads (i2cReadI2CBlockData) to fetch the 6 accelerometer bytes starting at 0x3B and the 6 gyroscope bytes starting at 0x43 efficiently, and log timestamped raw x, y, z accelerometer and gyroscope values to a CSV file named 'imu_log.csv' at 10 Hz (100 ms interval). Check the return value of every I2C operation and print failures to stderr, and handle Ctrl+C (SIGINT) gracefully by closing the I2C handle, terminating pigpio, and closing the CSV file before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads X, Y, and Z acceleration data from a GY-45 MMA8451Q accelerometer over I2C bus 1 at address 0x1D, using the Linux i2c-dev ioctl interface for I2C access (libgpiod has no I2C API) and libgpiod for the LED GPIO line on GPIO17 (BCM numbering) — never wiringPi. Verify the sensor's identity by reading the WHO_AM_I register (0x0D) and checking it equals 0x1A before operation. Poll the sensor every 100 ms and trigger the LED if the magnitude of acceleration on any axis exceeds a threshold of 2.0g, given the sensor's default +-2g range where 1g = 1024 counts; when an impact is detected, turn the LED on for 500 ms and append a timestamped entry to 'impact_log.txt'. Handle I2C read/write errors gracefully, and cleanly release all resources — the I2C bus, GPIO lines, and file handles — on SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads X, Y, and Z magnetic field data from a Texas Instruments TMAG5273 I2C 3D Hall-Effect sensor at its default address 0x35, using the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface directly (open/ioctl/read/write) rather than wiringPi, to simulate an industrial robotic arm joint position feedback system. Use 16-bit little-endian reads for the X, Y, and Z result registers at 0x10, 0x11, and 0x12, sampling once per second, and log the data with timestamps to 'magnetic_field_log.csv', writing the CSV header row on startup if the file does not already exist. Check every syscall (open, ioctl, read, write, fopen, etc.) and handle errors gracefully; if an I2C read fails, log an error to stderr and continue the loop. Implement a signal handler for SIGINT/SIGTERM that cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and the CSV file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a SparkFun ADXL345 I2C accelerometer on /dev/i2c-1 at address 0x53 via the Linux i2c-dev ioctl interface, and uses libgpiod (never wiringPi) to request a falling-edge interrupt on GPIO17 (physical pin 11), connected to the ADXL345 INT1 pin, to detect freefall events. Put the sensor in standby before register writes, then configure it: set THRESH_FF (0x0A) to ~300 mg, TIME_FF (0x20) to ~100 ms, enable the freefall interrupt via bit 2 of INT_ENABLE (0x2E), map it to INT1 via INT_MAP (0x2F = 0x00), and enter measurement mode by setting POWER_CTL (0x2D) to 0x08. On each interrupt, read INT_SOURCE (0x30) to verify the freefall bit (bit 2) is set, then read 6 bytes from DATAX0 (0x32) in a single I2C block read; reading INT_SOURCE also clears the interrupt. Log timestamped X, Y, Z acceleration values only during a freefall event to 'freefall_log.csv' in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.mmm,X,Y,Z' (with milliseconds), writing a header row on creation and flushing after each write. Check every I2C syscall and GPIO call, verify the device ID (register 0x00 should read 0xE5) at startup, and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths. Use a poll-based loop on the libgpiod event file descriptor rather than threads, and on SIGINT/SIGTERM disable the sensor's interrupts, close the I2C file descriptor, release the GPIO lines, close the chip, and close the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library for I2C to read accelerometer and gyroscope data from an STMicroelectronics LSM6DSR IMU on I2C bus 1 at address 0x6A (SDA=GPIO2, SCL=GPIO3), configured for +-2g accelerometer and +-250 dps gyroscope range at 104 Hz ODR. Log timestamped readings in CSV format to 'motion_log.txt' and implement a basic fall-detection state machine (IDLE -> FREEFALL -> IMPACT) using an acceleration-magnitude threshold below 0.2g for freefall and above 2.5g for impact within a 1.0 second window. Handle I2C read/write errors, a sensor-absent condition via a WHO_AM_I check, and bus errors gracefully, and ensure clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library for SPI and timing to interface with an Analog Devices ADIS16266 digital gyroscope over SPI channel 0 (CE0/GPIO8) at 1 MHz, SPI mode 3 (CPOL=1, CPHA=1), using 16-bit register access with a 2-byte transfer per register access and no dummy byte. The read command sends the register address with bit 7 set (0x80 OR), and the response is returned in the next transaction. Read the X_GYRO_OUT register (0x14) every 10 ms, scale the value at 0.0305 deg/sec/LSB, and log timestamped angular-rate readings in degrees/sec to 'gyro_log.csv', opened once at startup with a CSV header rather than reopened on every write. Check every pigpio SPI call's return value, verify the WHO_AM_I register (expected 0x3F5A or a device-specific ID) on startup, and print informative error messages on failure. Handle SIGINT gracefully by closing the SPI handle, terminating pigpio, and closing the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to continuously read X, Y, and Z angular velocities from a GY-50 L3G4200D gyroscope over I2C bus 1 at address 0x69. Configure the sensor for normal mode with all axes enabled (CTRL_REG1 = 0x0F) and +-250 dps full-scale range (CTRL_REG4 = 0x00). Read all 6 data bytes starting at OUT_X_L (0x28) in a single block read, and convert raw values to degrees per second using sensitivity 8.75 mdps/LSB (i.e., divide by 114.285). Log each sample with a nanosecond-precision timestamp to 'gyro_log.csv' with a header row 'Timestamp,X,Y,Z', sampling every 10 ms. Retry I2C writes up to 3 times during initialization, check every I2C call, verify the WHO_AM_I register (0x0F) reads 0xD3 before proceeding, and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths. Use signal handling for graceful termination, performing clean resource release on SIGINT by closing the I2C handle, closing the file, and calling gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that initializes the pigpio library and reads a KY-026 Flame Sensor Module's digital output connected to GPIO17 (physical pin 11), enabling the internal pull-up resistor on GPIO17 so the input is deterministic when the sensor's open-collector output is off. The DO line is active-LOW: it reads LOW (0) when a flame is detected and HIGH (1) when no flame is present. Check for pigpio initialization failure, then open 'flame_events.log' in append mode and verify the file handle is valid. In a main loop, poll the sensor every 500 ms; on each poll, log a timestamped line of the form 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS - Flame detected: YES|NO' to the log file and immediately flush it, and when a flame is detected (LOW), print 'FLAME DETECTED!' to the console to simulate a fire alarm. Install a SIGINT handler so Ctrl+C sets a flag that stops the loop cleanly, and on any exit path close the log file if open and call gpioTerminate(). Handle sensor read errors (gpioRead returning PI_BAD_GPIO) by logging an error line rather than a false positive.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that interfaces with an Omron D7S-0001 vibration sensor over I2C at slave address 0x53 on bus /dev/i2c-1, using the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface directly (open/read/ioctl) rather than wiringPi, to simulate a structural integrity monitoring system. The D7S-0001 exposes acceleration in registers 0x28-0x2D (X_LSB, X_MSB, Y_LSB, Y_MSB, Z_LSB, Z_MSB); combine each axis as signed 16-bit (MSB<<8 | LSB). Sample the sensor every 100 ms and log X, Y, and Z axis acceleration data to a CSV file named 'vibration_log.csv' with header 'Timestamp,X,Y,Z' and ISO-8601 UTC timestamps. Check every open/ioctl/read call, detect sensor-absent paths (e.g. an I2C read returning 0xFF or failing), and handle bus errors gracefully without crashing; if a read fails, print a diagnostic to stderr and skip that sample rather than terminating. Install a SIGINT handler so Ctrl+C cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and the CSV file before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses libgpiod (v1.6+ API) to monitor a conveyor belt safety system by reading the digital output of two TI DRV5032 digital Hall-Effect sensors connected to GPIO17 and GPIO27, configured as inputs with internal pull-ups enabled via bias flags. Log timestamps with millisecond precision and the sensor states to 'conveyor_log.txt' every 50 ms, and if both sensors read logic 1 (triggered), halt the conveyor, simulated with a print statement. Include robust error handling for GPIO access (chip opening, line requests, reads) and log file I/O, and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, releasing all libgpiod resources cleanly on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running a 64-bit OS that interfaces with a GY-45 MMA8452Q 3-axis accelerometer over I2C using the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface (no third-party GPIO/I2C libraries such as wiringPi). The sensor's SA0 pin is tied high, so use I2C address 0x1D on bus /dev/i2c-1. Verify the sensor identity by reading the WHO_AM_I register (0x0D) and checking it equals 0x2A, printing an error and exiting if it does not match. Initialize the sensor by reading CTRL_REG1 (0x2A), clearing bit 0 to place it in standby mode, setting the data rate to 100 Hz (bits 3-5 = 0b010), and then setting bit 0 to switch to active mode. Continuously poll the accelerometer at roughly 100 Hz (10 ms loop interval), reading the six data registers (0x01-0x06) in a single I2C block read for atomic sampling, combining MSB/LSB and right-shifting by 4 to form signed 12-bit values, and compute the tilt angle of the X-axis relative to gravity using atan2(x, sqrt(y*y + z*z)). When the absolute tilt angle exceeds 45 degrees, log a timestamped line containing the raw 12-bit X, Y, Z values to fall_log.txt, opened once in append mode at startup. Handle all I2C syscall failures (open, ioctl, read, write) by printing strerror(errno) and exiting or skipping the iteration as appropriate. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that closes the I2C file descriptor and the log file before exiting, keeping the log file open for the program's lifetime and flushing after each entry rather than reopening it on every write.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with an Adafruit LIS3MDL Triple-Axis Magnetometer over I2C on /dev/i2c-1 at address 0x1E, using the Linux i2c-dev ioctl interface for I2C access since libgpiod has no I2C API. Configure the sensor for continuous-conversion mode at 80 Hz ODR with high-performance mode on all axes (CTRL_REG1=0x70, CTRL_REG4=0x0C, CTRL_REG3=0x00), and verify the sensor is present by reading WHO_AM_I (0x0F) and checking it equals 0x3D. Continuously read the 6-byte little-endian X/Y/Z magnetic-field output registers starting at 0x28, apply fixed offset/scale calibration constants, convert to milliGauss using the +-4 gauss sensitivity of 0.146 mG/LSB, and append comma-separated X,Y,Z values to 'magnetic_log.txt' at 10 Hz. Check every I2C read/write for errors and retry initialization up to 3 times; handle SIGINT/SIGTERM cleanly by closing the I2C file descriptor and the log file, which should be opened once and flushed after each write. Include a simple metal-detector threshold alert printed to stderr when the total field magnitude exceeds 800 mG.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library over SPI channel 0 (CE0/GPIO8), 1 MHz clock, SPI Mode 0, to read acceleration data from an Analog Devices ADXL354B accelerometer. The ADXL354B outputs 20-bit signed acceleration data in 3 consecutive bytes per axis (XDATA at 0x08, YDATA at 0x0B, ZDATA at 0x0E); use the +-2g range sensitivity of 3.9 microg/LSB (0.0000039 g/LSB). SPI reads use bit 7 = 1 for read and bit 6 = 1 for multi-byte. Implement a proper device reset sequence: write 0x52 to the RESET register (0x1F), wait 1 ms, then set the measurement mode by clearing the RUN bit in POWER_CTL (0x2D), waiting for the STABLE bit in STATUS (0x04), then setting the RUN bit. Log X, Y, and Z axis readings with timestamps every 100 ms to a file named 'vibration_log.txt'. Handle SPI communication errors with retries, check sensor presence by reading PARTID (0x01, expected 0x1D), and implement graceful shutdown via SIGINT/SIGTERM with proper resource cleanup: close the SPI handle, close the file, and terminate pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library's spiOpen and spiXfer APIs (not deprecated wiringPi) to interface with an Analog Devices ADIS16362 IMU over SPI channel 0 (CE0/GPIO8), baud rate 1 MHz, SPI Mode 3 (active-high clock, sampled on trailing edge). The ADIS16362 read protocol sends the register address with the MSB set followed by a dummy byte, with the requested register's data returned on the next 16-bit transfer; implement a robust read function that sends the address, waits for the conversion, and retrieves the data, handling stall/error returns from spiXfer. Continuously read 3-axis gyroscope from X_GYRO=0x04, Y_GYRO=0x06, Z_GYRO=0x08 and 3-axis accelerometer from X_ACCL=0x0A, Y_ACCL=0x0C, Z_ACCL=0x0E, scaling with 0.05 deg/sec/LSB for gyroscope and 0.0025 g/LSB for accelerometer, sampling at approximately 100 Hz (10 ms delay between reads). Log timestamped readings to a comma-separated file 'imu_log.csv' starting with the header 'Timestamp,X_Gyro,Y_Gyro,Z_Gyro,X_Accel,Y_Accel,Z_Accel', using high-precision UNIX epoch timestamps (seconds.nanoseconds). Check pigpio initialization, SPI open, file open, and spiXfer return codes; if spiXfer fails, print an error to stderr and skip the logging iteration. Implement graceful shutdown via SIGINT (Ctrl+C) using a signal handler that safely closes the SPI handle, flushes and closes the log file, and calls gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library (not the deprecated sysfs interface, and not wiringPi) to read an E18-D80NK IR obstacle sensor connected to GPIO17. The E18-D80NK outputs LOW (0) when an obstacle is detected within its detection range, adjustable up to about 80 cm and configured here for roughly 30 cm, and HIGH (1) when the path is clear. Open the gpiochip device for GPIO17 on the Raspberry Pi 5 (gpiochip4) and request the line for input direction using modern libgpiod APIs such as gpiod_chip_open_by_name, gpiod_line_open, gpiod_line_request_input, and gpiod_line_get_value. Poll the sensor every 1 second; when an obstacle is detected (line reads LOW), trigger a simulated "self-parking" sequence logged to the console with timestamps ("Self-parking sequence started" / "completed"). Check all libgpiod calls, handle the case where the gpiochip or line is unavailable and exit gracefully, and handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) for clean shutdown, releasing the GPIO line and closing the chip on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses libgpiod (v2 API) to interface with two Keyes KY-032 IR obstacle avoidance sensors connected to GPIO17 and GPIO27 (physical pins 11 and 13, BCM numbering). The KY-032 output is active-low: the sensor reads 0 when an obstacle is detected and 1 when the path is clear. Use a single gpiochip and request both lines together for input, reading both lines in a single call via the libgpiod v2 bulk-read API gpiod_line_request_get_values. Poll both sensors every 100 ms and log the obstacle detection status to the console with a timestamp, simulating a basic collision avoidance system for a small robot, running in an infinite loop until interrupted. Check every libgpiod call, handle the case where the gpiochip or lines are unavailable, and ensure clean release of all resources on all exit paths including SIGINT (Ctrl+C). Compile cleanly with -Wall -Wextra against libgpiod >= 2.0.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the modern libgpiod library for SPI chip-select line control together with the Linux spidev interface for SPI communication (not the deprecated bcm2835 or wiringPi libraries) to periodically read gyroscope data from an Analog Devices ADIS16266 connected on SPI0 (CE0 on GPIO8), configured for SPI Mode 3, MSB first, at a 1 MHz clock speed. Initialize the SPI device (/dev/spidev0.0) and a libgpiod line for the CS pin, write to the MSC_CTRL register (0x24) to enable data ready mode, then periodically read the X, Y, and Z angular rate output registers (0x04, 0x06, 0x08) using the ADIS16266 two-transfer read protocol (send the address with the MSB set, then read 2 bytes). Convert the raw 16-bit signed values to angular rates using the scale factor of 0.02 deg/sec/LSB and log the results to the console every 100 ms. Include robust error handling: check all SPI and GPIO initialization calls, handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT, running in a loop until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses only the pigpio C API, not wiringPi, to read accelerometer and gyroscope data from an STMicroelectronics LSM6DSR connected via I2C bus 1 at the 7-bit address 0x6B. Initialize the pigpio library and open the I2C bus, then verify the sensor is present by reading the WHO_AM_I register and checking it returns 0x6B. Configure the accelerometer for +-2g full-scale at 104 Hz (CTRL1_XL = 0x42) and the gyroscope for +-250 dps at 104 Hz (CTRL2_G = 0x42). Every 100 ms, burst-read 12 bytes starting at OUTX_L_G (0x22) covering gyro X/Y/Z then accel X/Y/Z, convert to physical units using gyro sensitivity mdps/LSB = 8.75 (i.e. 0.00875 dps/LSB) and accel sensitivity mg/LSB = 0.061 (i.e. 0.000061 g/LSB), and print one line to stdout. Handle all error paths: pigpio init failure, I2C open failure, WHO_AM_I mismatch, register write failures, and short or failed burst reads, printing to stderr and exiting non-zero; check every I2C call's return value and never use hard-coded sleeps that ignore errors. Install a SIGINT handler so Ctrl+C triggers a clean shutdown that closes the I2C handle and calls gpioTerminate() before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to read accelerometer and magnetometer data from an Adafruit FXOS8700 breakout board over I2C at address 0x1D on bus 1 (GPIO2/GPIO3 for SDA/SCL). Initialize the sensor into hybrid mode by configuring CTRL_REG1 (0x2A), CTRL_REG2 (0x2B), M_CTRL_REG1 (0x5B), and M_CTRL_REG2 (0x5C) so both the accelerometer and magnetometer produce data. Every 100 ms, read the 12-byte combined data block starting at register 0x01 (OUT_X_MSB), which contains 6 bytes of 14-bit left-aligned accelerometer data followed by 6 bytes of 16-bit magnetometer data, and log the raw X, Y, and Z values for both sensors to the console each cycle. Handle I2C communication errors robustly: check every pigpio I2C call, verify the sensor is present by reading the WHO_AM_I register (0x0D, expected value 0xC7) before initialization, and retry on transient read failures. Clean up all resources — close the I2C handle and terminate pigpio — on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that interfaces with an ADXL345 accelerometer over I2C at address 0x53 using the Linux i2c-dev interface via /dev/i2c-1, not wiringPi, since libgpiod itself has no I2C API. Read X, Y, Z data from registers 0x32-0x37, calculate tilt angles using atan2, and log events with timestamps every 100 ms. Log tilt events exceeding a threshold of 30.0 degrees to '/var/log/tilt_events.log'. Include robust error handling for I2C communication failures, explicitly handling sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for Ctrl+C.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library, and no wiringPi, to monitor ambient noise levels via a KY-038 sound sensor connected to GPIO17 (physical pin 11). The KY-038 OUT pin is active-high and pulses when sound exceeds its onboard comparator threshold. Accept a single command-line argument — an integer threshold representing the minimum number of high-readings per 5-second window required to trigger an alert — and validate it, rejecting non-numeric or non-positive values. Continuously sample GPIO17 every 1 ms for 5 seconds, counting how many times the pin reads high; at the end of each 5-second window, print a timestamped ALERT to stdout if the high-reading count exceeds the threshold, otherwise print a normal status line. Run in a continuous loop until signaled to stop, with a 1-second pause between monitoring windows. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully, terminating pigpio and exiting cleanly, and check every pigpio call for failure (gpioInitialise, gpioSetMode), printing clear error messages to stderr on any failure.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the libgpiod C API, never wiringPi, to control two 12V electromagnetic door locks actuated by 5V active-HIGH relay modules driven via TIP120 transistors on GPIO17 (Door A) and GPIO27 (Door B), based on a randomly generated 6-digit security code. Initialize GPIO17 and GPIO27 as outputs, both defaulting to LOW (locks energized/closed); a HIGH signal de-energizes the relay and unlocks the corresponding door. Generate a random 6-digit code between 100000 and 999999 at startup and print it to stdout. In a loop, prompt the user to enter the code via stdin; if it matches, unlock Door A (GPIO17 HIGH) for 5 seconds, then re-lock it (LOW), log the successful entry to 'access_log.txt' as a CSV row 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,NNNNNN', and generate a new random code. If the code does not match, print 'Access denied' and continue; handle invalid non-numeric stdin input gracefully by clearing the buffer and re-prompting. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag so the main loop exits cleanly; on exit, drive both GPIO outputs LOW (locked), release all libgpiod resources (lines and chip), and close any open file handles. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the standard Linux /dev/i2c-1 ioctl interface, not the unmaintained bcm2835 library, to read illuminance from a BH1750FVI light sensor over I2C bus 1 (GPIO2/GPIO3). The sensor's ADDR pin is tied to GND, so the I2C address is 0x23. Write the One-Time High-Resolution Mode 2 command (0x21) to the sensor, wait for the maximum conversion time of 180 ms, then read 2 bytes of data and calculate the illuminance in lux using the formula: (raw_value * 5) / 6 (equivalent to raw_value / 1.2). Log the sensor readings to a file named 'light_log.txt', formatting each entry as 'Timestamp: <timestamp>, Lux: <lux_value>', continuously every 5 seconds until interrupted. The program must handle potential I2C write/read errors and sensor-absent paths (e.g., failing to open the bus or read bytes), and implement clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT (Ctrl+C).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses pigpio for I2C and hardware PWM to implement a theremin using an MPR121 capacitive touch sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x5A. The program acts as a TCP server listening on port 12345; when a client sends a message starting with 'MOTION_DETECTED:' and containing the shared secret 'MySecretKey', the theremin plays tones for 5 seconds based on capacitive touch readings, using hardware PWM on GPIO18. Initialize the MPR121 with proper soft-reset and electrode configuration, and map the maximum electrode filtered data value to a frequency in the range 220-880 Hz using a logarithmic scale, sampling touch values every 20 ms during the 5-second playback window and logging each frequency to 'frequency_log.txt'. Handle errors for pigpio initialization, I2C open/read, and socket/bind/listen/accept. On SIGINT/SIGTERM, stop PWM, close I2C and sockets, and terminate pigpio cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with an LSM303DLHC magnetometer via I2C bus 1 at default address 0x1E, connected to the physical SDA1/SCL1 pins, and controls an LED on GPIO17. Use libgpiod for GPIO/PWM control and the standard Linux I2C interface (/dev/i2c-1, ioctl) for sensor communication, not wiringPi. Initialize the magnetometer by writing 0x18 to CTRL_REG1_M (0x20) for 10 Hz continuous conversion, and read 6 bytes of data starting from OUT_X_L_M (0x08) in a single I2C block read. The program must read X, Y, Z magnetic field data, compute the magnitude of the Z-axis field, and adjust the LED brightness proportionally using hardware PWM, sampling every 100 ms in the main loop. Handle I2C errors (e.g., sensor absent, bus errors) gracefully by logging the error and skipping the sample without crashing, and implement clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM by releasing the PWM, closing the I2C file descriptor, and closing any log files.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to interface with an HMC5883L magnetometer via I2C on bus 1 at address 0x1E. Configure the sensor for 8-sample averaging, 15 Hz output rate, and a gain setting of 1.3 Gauss (Configuration Register A = 0x70, Configuration Register B = 0x20, Mode register = 0x00 for continuous mode). Continuously collect raw readings to compute hard-iron offsets as a running average over a 100-sample window. Every 500 ms, apply the current hard-iron offsets to the latest raw reading and print the offset-corrected (not unit-normalized) X, Y, and Z values to stdout. Explicitly flag any I2C read/write errors on stderr without crashing, and ensure clean resource release of the I2C handle and pigpio library on SIGINT/SIGTERM. Do not use FIFOs or secondary processes.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads tri-axial acceleration data from an LSM303D accelerometer/magnetometer connected via I2C at address 0x1D (SA0 tied high) on /dev/i2c-1, using the Linux i2c-dev kernel API (open, ioctl I2C_SLAVE, i2c_smbus_read_byte_data, i2c_smbus_write_byte_data, i2c_smbus_read_i2c_block_data) for I2C communication, not wiringPi, and the libgpiod library for the GPIO interrupt line request and event monitoring, not wiringPiISR. The LSM303D's INT1 pin is connected to GPIO23 (BCM pin 23, physical pin 16). Verify the WHO_AM_I register (0x0F) reads 0x49 before proceeding, then configure the accelerometer for 50 Hz ODR with all axes enabled (CTRL_REG1 = 0x57), full-scale +-2g (CTRL_REG4 = 0x00, sensitivity 0.061 mg/LSB), and a threshold interrupt on any-axis-high event (INT1_CFG = 0x2A) with threshold 2000 mg (register value = 2000/16 = 125 = 0x7D) and duration 0 (immediate). Use a 6-byte multi-byte burst read from OUT_X_L_A (0x28) with auto-increment (MSB of the register address set to 0x80). Poll acceleration at roughly 10 ms intervals and store each sample in a 64-entry in-memory circular buffer; on a rising edge of the INT1 GPIO interrupt, print a timestamp and dump the last 10 buffered samples. Check every I2C read/write and file-open call, printing a diagnostic to stderr and exiting non-zero on initialization failure; if a runtime I2C read fails, print a warning to stderr and skip that sample without corrupting the buffer. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library, never wiringPi, to actuate two 12V DC push-pull solenoids in an alternating sequence with a 500 ms delay between each transition, simulating a simple reciprocating linear actuator for a miniature automated assembly line prototype. Solenoid 1 is driven via a TIP120 transistor on GPIO17 (BCM numbering); solenoid 2 via a TIP120 transistor on GPIO27 (BCM numbering); both circuits include flyback diodes. Before entering the main loop, drive both lines LOW so no solenoid is energized at startup. In the loop, alternate: energize solenoid 1 for 500 ms, then de-energize solenoid 1 and energize solenoid 2 for 500 ms, then de-energize solenoid 2, using nanosleep for the timing. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so Ctrl+C cleanly releases both lines (sets them LOW) and frees all libgpiod resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to control two 12V electromagnetic door locks via GPIO17 and GPIO27 (active-HIGH relay modules), implementing a dual-factor authentication system where both locks open only after receiving a specific, pre-defined, matching 6-digit code via two separate UART serial inputs: /dev/serial0 (primary UART, GPIO14/15) and /dev/serial1 (secondary UART), at 9600 baud with 8N1 framing. The expected code is '123456'. Initialize pigpio and configure GPIO17 and GPIO27 as outputs, defaulting to LOW (locked) on startup and on every exit path. Read 6-digit numeric codes from each UART with a 5-second per-port timeout, resetting the input buffer on non-digit characters, and poll both serial ports in a single main loop with non-blocking reads so codes can arrive in any order within the timeout window. Unlock both doors simultaneously (set both GPIOs HIGH) for 2 seconds, then re-lock (set both GPIOs LOW), only when both received codes match each other and match the expected code, using constant-time string comparison to avoid timing side-channels. Handle errors for pigpio initialization failure, serial port open failure, serial read timeouts, and GPIO write failures, logging each to stderr. Implement clean shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM: ensure both locks are set to LOW (locked), close the serial handles, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the modern libgpiod API (gpiod_line_request_input, gpiod_line_request_output, gpiod_line_get_value, gpiod_line_set_value), not wiringPi, to control a 5V relay connected to physical GPIO17 upon detecting motion from an HC-SR501 PIR sensor on physical GPIO4, simulating a door strike. Open the gpiochip by name (gpiochip0) and request the two lines explicitly, checking every libgpiod call for errors and logging failures to the system journal via syslog(3). When motion is detected (PIR reads HIGH), energize the relay (drive GPIO17 HIGH) for a 1-second strike duration, then de-energize it (LOW), polling the PIR pin every 50 ms. As a failsafe, if the PIR sensor remains HIGH for more than 10 seconds continuously, de-energize the relay and log a LOG_WARNING entry to the system journal describing a potential malfunction. Log all state transitions (motion detected, relay on/off, failsafe trigger, shutdown) via syslog. Implement clean shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM: release all GPIO lines, close the chip, close the log, and exit, ensuring the relay is driven LOW before releasing the line.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to control a 4-channel active-LOW relay module connected to GPIO4, GPIO17, GPIO27, and GPIO22, implementing a timed sequence to simulate a simple automated irrigation system. The relay module is active-LOW (LOW = ON, HIGH = OFF); initialize all relays to OFF (HIGH) at startup. Activate each relay sequentially for 5 minutes (300 seconds), with a 1-minute (60 seconds) pause between each activation, looping back to the 1st relay after the 4th. Log every relay state change (activation and deactivation) with timestamps to the system syslog using openlog/syslog with the identifier 'irrigation_system'; do not use UDP networking. Check every pigpio call (gpioInitialise, gpioSetMode, gpioWrite, gpioSetTimerFuncEx) and log failures to syslog before exiting cleanly. Use gpioSetTimerFuncEx with a single timer (timer 0) that fires every 60 seconds, maintaining an internal state machine that tracks whether the current action is a relay activation, deactivation, or pause, and keep the program alive with a sleep loop checking a volatile sig_atomic_t flag. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM: deactivate all relays (set HIGH), release GPIO resources via gpioTerminate(), close syslog, and exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads acceleration data from an MPU6050 connected via I2C at default address 0x68 on bus /dev/i2c-1, opening the I2C device directly with open()/ioctl() rather than wiringPi. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library (v1 API), not the deprecated wiringPi library, to control four 5V relay modules connected to physical GPIO pins 18, 23, 24, and 25 (BCM numbering), simulating a smart lighting system that toggles each light based on a unique prime number interval: 2, 3, 5, and 7 seconds respectively. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to monitor a KY-038 sound sensor's digital OUT pin connected to GPIO17.
